title: Planning backwards from what students need to learn
intro: Use this when a lesson contains worthwhile activities but the knowledge students should leave with is unclear. Start with the intended learning, then select the explanation, practice and checks that will build it.
tips: Write the final response first. An exemplar exposes the vocabulary, reasoning and component knowledge students will need.
Plan the learning episode. A new idea may need part of a lesson or several lessons; the timetable is not the learning sequence.
Plan the check alongside the task. Decide what a successful response would demonstrate before choosing slides or worksheets.
Keep useful difficulty. Remove logistical obstacles without removing the thinking needed to reach the endpoint.
Plan beyond first success. Build in later retrieval and a less familiar application so today’s performance is revisited.
script: “By the end of this sequence, you will explain which material is suitable and justify your choice using its properties.”
do: Align the question, explanation and practice with the same learning.
Change the route when a prerequisite is insecure.
avoid: Planning an activity sequence before defining the learning.
Treating a completed product as evidence that every component is understood.
steps: Specify the endpoint. Describe what students will know or do independently, including the quality of explanation or performance required.
Unpack the demand. List the prerequisite knowledge and genuinely new components; identify which missing component would prevent success.
Plan the route. Sequence a clear model, supported rehearsal, accurate independent practice and a purposeful variation.
Plan decision points. Select questions that will reveal whether students are ready for each increase in demand, with a likely response to common errors.
Prepare the resources last. Keep only material that supports the route, and schedule later opportunities to retrieve and apply the learning.
example: In History, the endpoint is an explanation of why one factor contributed to an event. Planning begins with the expected causal reasoning and evidence. The teacher identifies the factual knowledge students need, models a causal paragraph, checks the link between claim and evidence, then sets a different factor for practice. The worksheet follows that sequence rather than determining it.

title: Prerequisite knowledge checks: identifying the foundations for new learning
intro: Use this before new teaching when students need specific existing knowledge to access the explanation. Check the actual prerequisite rather than asking whether students remember last lesson.
tips: Atomise the check. Test a small prerequisite directly, rather than hiding it inside a complex question that makes failure hard to interpret.
Separate recall from application. A remembered definition does not automatically establish that students can use it.
Choose a consequential prerequisite. Check the knowledge that would block today’s learning, not everything previously taught.
Fix the gap before adding complexity. A brief model and a fresh check may be more useful than continuing over an insecure foundation.
Keep the BSCS boundary clear. Spaced retrieval belongs in Do Now; the immediate prerequisite check sits at the opening of Explain.
script: “Before we explain ionic formulae, show me the charge on a magnesium ion and a chloride ion. Keep your answers private until the signal.”
do: Gather independent responses before introducing the new demand.
Make the connection to new learning explicit.
avoid: Inferring readiness from confident volunteers.
Repeating an entire previous lesson when one component needs repair.
steps: Identify the prerequisite. Name the small piece of knowledge or process that students must retrieve before the new content can make sense.
Elicit it from everyone. Use a short atomised question, mini-whiteboards, call and response or a brief written response. Check competence, not confidence.
State the connection. Explain how the new learning builds on what students already know; highlight similarities and differences.
Start broad, then narrow. Give the general concept or organising idea before introducing detail.
Make students process the link. Use self-explanation, Turn and Talk or a comparison prompt so pupils articulate the connection themselves.
Check meaning and revisit. Probe how ideas connect, address weak links, and return to the concept later so the connection remains accessible.
example: Before teaching ionic formulae, a Chemistry teacher checks ion charges on boards. Several pupils remember the symbols but confuse charges. The teacher repairs that small prerequisite and checks another pair of ions before modelling charge balance. The new explanation now starts from knowledge the class has shown it can use.

title: Anticipating misconceptions and planning how to uncover them
intro: Use this when students repeatedly make the same plausible error. Anticipate the reasoning behind that error so the lesson exposes and repairs it rather than merely announcing the correct answer.
tips: Use real errors. Student work is a better source of plausible misconceptions than invented distractors with no likely rationale.
Separate slips from beliefs. Ask how the answer was reached before assuming a conceptual misconception.
Plan a near-miss. A convincing wrong example can make the critical distinction visible.
Keep the correction focused. Repair the faulty rule or decision rather than explaining every part of the topic again.
Recheck with changed surface features. Students need to apply the repaired idea, not repeat the exact answer they just heard.
script: “Someone says heavier objects always fall faster. Which part of that claim needs testing? Explain what evidence would settle it.”
do: Name the misconception each planned answer would reveal.
Prepare a contrasting example and follow-up question.
avoid: Calling every incorrect answer a misconception.
Revealing the solution before finding out students’ reasoning.
steps: Start from the intended idea. Write the accurate rule, relationship or distinction students need to understand.
Predict the wrong model. Describe what a student might reasonably believe and why that would produce the error.
Design the diagnostic prompt. Use a choice, comparison, explanation or short task that distinguishes the correct and incorrect reasoning.
Prepare the repair. Select an example and non-example, model or demonstration that addresses the precise difference.
Plan the fresh check. Change the context enough to require thinking while retaining the concept you are checking.
example: In Geography, a teacher anticipates the belief that weather and climate mean the same thing. Students classify statements about a single day and long-term patterns. Their explanations reveal whether the distinction is secure. The teacher contrasts the timescales explicitly, then gives new statements so pupils apply the repaired distinction.

title: Diagnostic questions: planning questions that reveal understanding
intro: Use diagnostic questions when you need to see which misconception or decision is causing difficulty. A well-designed wrong option tells you something useful about students’ thinking.
tips: Make distractors diagnostic. Each wrong option should arise from a recognisable error you could respond to.
Avoid accidental clues. Option length, grammar or an implausible answer should not give away the correct choice.
Generate before recognising. Where appropriate, hide the options first so students attempt an answer before selecting.
Investigate wrong options. Ask why a student might choose them, or how to alter an option to make it correct.
Inspect correct reasoning too. A correct choice can come from guessing or a faulty method; probe selected explanations.
script: “Work out your answer first. Now compare it with the four options. Choose privately and prepare to explain which feature rules out the others.”
do: Use one unambiguously correct answer.
Interpret the pattern of distractors before deciding the response.
avoid: Writing arbitrary wrong options to fill the spaces.
Treating the percentage correct as the whole diagnosis.
steps: Specify the knowledge. Target one important idea, decision or misconception; minimise unrelated reading and calculation demands.
Build the options. Write the correct response and plausible distractors, recording the reasoning each distractor would indicate.
Protect independent commitment. Explain the response method first, allow silent thinking and collect everyone’s choice before revealing any answer.
Probe the pattern. Ask selected students for their reasoning, including some who chose correctly; compare alternatives without shaming individuals.
Act on the diagnosis. Reteach the identified distinction, use discussion where students have something useful to compare, and ask a fresh related question.
example: A Maths teacher designs options from likely errors in calculating a percentage reduction: subtracting the percentage as a number, retaining the original amount, or calculating only the reduction. The distribution reveals which decision needs teaching. Students explain a wrong option before completing a fresh calculation, rather than simply being told which letter is correct.

title: Scaffolding: preparing support and deciding when to remove it

links.label: DistillED - Provide Scaffolds for Difficult Tasks

intro: Use a scaffold when a specific barrier prevents students from attempting the intended learning successfully. Keep the goal clear and plan how students will work without the support.
tips: Name the barrier. Decide whether the student needs help with knowledge, language, organisation or a particular process step.
Scaffold the obstacle. A vocabulary bank helps with expression; it will not repair an untaught concept.
Make support optional where appropriate. Students who can already work independently should not have to complete unnecessary scaffolding.
Preserve the decision. Give a starting cue or structure without supplying the thinking the task is meant to develop.
Plan the withdrawal. Decide what successful performance would justify removing a cue, worked step or sentence frame.
script: “Use this opening frame to state your claim. You will choose the evidence and explain the link yourself; the frame does not supply those decisions.”
do: Match temporary support to the diagnosed need.
Keep the curricular goal ambitious.
avoid: Assigning a permanent scaffold by pupil label.
Removing every support at once because time has passed.
steps: Diagnose the barrier. Identify whether pupils lack knowledge, cannot coordinate the steps, are overloaded by presentation, or need a cue to select a known process.
Break the process into meaningful steps. Sequence the task so pupils can focus on one decision at a time while still seeing how the parts contribute to the whole.
Select a targeted support. Use a model, worked example, prompt, frame, word bank, visual cue, checklist or partially completed response that addresses the diagnosed barrier.
Keep the thinking with the pupil. The scaffold should cue attention or structure action; it should not complete the crucial reasoning on the pupil's behalf.
Check and adjust. Use responses during practice to decide whether to re-model, retain, reduce or remove the support.
Plan the fade before use. Decide which element will disappear first and what evidence will indicate readiness for the next level of independence.
example: In English, pupils need to explain how evidence supports a claim. A frame supplies the paragraph structure while pupils choose and interpret the quotation. Once they can build the link, the opening phrases are removed. The scaffold supports expression without replacing the interpretation that the task is intended to develop.

title: Entry routines: establishing a purposeful start
intro: Use the agreed BSCS entry routine to make the move from corridor to independent learning warm, predictable and purposeful. Students should know where to go, what to prepare and how to begin.
tips: Prepare before entry. Display a Do Now that students can start without an explanation and have resources ready.
Keep the threshold position. Welcome students while monitoring the corridor and the developing classroom routine until the class is established.
Start the timer from first entry. Use the agreed three-to-five-minute window and build productive urgency.
Narrate the useful action. Recognise students beginning the task, rather than making general comments about being good.
Rehearse the exact sticking point. If equipment or movement causes repeated delay, practise that component rather than changing the whole routine.
script: “Good morning. Equipment ready. Straight to your seat and begin the Do Now silently. You have four minutes.”
do: Combine a warm greeting with clear expectations.
Correct briefly and precisely while protecting the start.
avoid: Using entry as an unplanned settling period.
Beginning an explanation while students are still moving or gathering equipment.
steps: Prepare the start. Display the Do Now and have the required resources ready before students arrive.
Welcome from the threshold. Establish the agreed queue and entry expectations while monitoring the corridor and classroom.
Release to the task. Students go to allocated seats, prepare equipment and begin silently; start the timer from first entry.
Maintain the entry position. Greet students and monitor the developing routine until a critical mass is established, using brief precise corrections.
Secure independent thinking. Narrate successful actions, complete the register when settled and use the agreed signal before reviewing the Do Now.
example: For a class arriving after lunch, the teacher displays four retrieval questions, has equipment ready and greets students at the threshold. The timer begins as the first pupils enter. Brief corrections address the exact entry action while the majority begin silently. The teacher moves into review only after using the agreed attention signal.

title: Teaching and rehearsing classroom routines
intro: Use this when a repeated classroom process is unreliable. Routines become useful when students understand, practise and rehearse the exact actions, rather than hear a rule once.
tips: Give the routine a learning purpose. Explain how it protects attention, safety or time, using language students understand.
Teach the cue and response together. Students need to recognise when the routine starts as well as what to do.
Show a convincing non-example. Make the difference visible without turning a pupil’s mistake into public entertainment.
Practise before content matters. Rehearse with an easy task so students can attend to the mechanics.
Revisit after drift. A short reset after holidays or repeated breakdown is usually better than increasingly lengthy reminders.
script: “We are practising the move from partner talk to listening. At the signal, finish the word you are saying, stop talking and put your pen down.”
do: Give feedback on an observable action.
Repeat the part that was not secure.
avoid: Assuming older students already know the routine.
Replacing the cue every time the routine is imperfect.
steps: Specify the actions. Break the routine into a short sequence with a clear starting cue and ending condition.
Explain and model. State why it matters, demonstrate success and show the common mistake students must avoid.
Rehearse together. Practise the process with low-demand content, watching the whole class for the precise point of breakdown.
Give focused feedback. Name what worked, correct one component and repeat it until the class can perform the sequence fluently.
Maintain the habit. Use the same cue, recognise successful execution and re-teach briefly when the routine drifts.
example: A Music teacher teaches how to move from listening to using instruments. Students practise collecting one instrument, waiting with hands still and starting on the cue. When premature playing reappears, the teacher rehearses that part briefly with an easy rhythm. The musical content can then proceed without competing with an uncertain equipment routine.

title: Signal for attention: securing readiness before teaching
intro: Use the agreed BSCS signal before instructions, explanations and transitions. Secure readiness before speaking so the beginning of the message reaches the whole class.
tips: Prime the transition. Tell students when they will stop and what readiness will look like before using the signal.
Choose a visible position. Stand where you can see every area and students can see you.
Be seen looking. Scan deliberately; your attention should communicate that you are checking the response.
Wait before academic talk. The signal loses meaning if the explanation starts while conversations or movement continue.
Follow with a listening check. Readiness gives students access to the message; recalling a key instruction shows whether it was received.
script: “In ten seconds, stop and get Focus Ready.” [Use the agreed BSCS signal.] “Thank you. First, write the title. What is the first action?”
do: Use the current shared BSCS cue consistently.
Correct the smallest remaining issue calmly.
avoid: Speaking over partial attention.
Treating eyes towards you as proof that the explanation was understood.
steps: Prime the transition. State when students will stop and what readiness will look like, before the attention signal.
Position visibly. Stand where all students can see you and you can observe the whole room.
Use the agreed BSCS signal. Give the current Focus Ready cue consistently and allow students to respond.
Pause and scan. Wait for the class to be ready; use a brief, precise correction for the remaining issue.
Give the message and check listening. Deliver a concise instruction or explanation, then ask students to retrieve the key action or point.
example: During partner discussion, the teacher primes the stop, moves where all pupils are visible and uses the agreed signal. The teacher waits and corrects two unfinished conversations before giving the instruction. A listening check establishes that students know the first next action. The transition does not begin with several pupils missing the message.

title: Checks for listening: instructions, explanations and classmates
intro: Use brief checks to establish whether students heard the instruction, key explanation point or contribution from a classmate. This helps distinguish missed information from difficulty understanding it.
tips: Teach the distinction. Explain that this question checks what was just said; a later task will check whether students can apply it.
Use Explain–Frame–Reframe. State a key relationship, ask students to complete it, then reverse the prompt where the reversal remains accurate.
Check peers’ contributions. Ask another student to restate the idea before inviting agreement, challenge or elaboration.
Make the message accessible first. Secure quiet, speak audibly and avoid distributing resources or introducing competing text while delivering it.
Keep corrections supportive. Restate the short message and give another opportunity; hearing, language or processing difficulties must not be treated as deliberate inattention.
script: “A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up. A catalyst speeds up…? Something that speeds up a reaction without being used up is…?”
do: Check instructions, explanations and classmates.
Ask a separate application question afterwards.
avoid: Using “Are you listening?” as the check.
Assuming successful repetition establishes understanding.
steps: Plan the message. Identify the exact instruction, definition or relationship students need to retain and make it concise.
Establish the routine. Explain why listening will be checked, secure attention and deliver the message without competing activity.
Ask for recall. Use question–pause–name, choral response or a brief written response to retrieve what was actually said.
Repair the missed point. Re-deliver or reframe it clearly, then check again; ask students to paraphrase a peer’s contribution where appropriate.
Move to understanding. Give a fresh question requiring application or explanation. Students can repeat accurately while remaining unsure how to use the idea.
example: An English teacher explains that the claim must be supported with a quotation. A pupil states where the evidence should appear, then another restates the key point from a classmate’s answer. Those checks establish receipt. A new paragraph task then tests whether students can select suitable evidence and explain the connection independently.

title: Behaviour scripts: correcting calmly and precisely
intro: Use calm, precise behaviour language to restore learning while preserving relationships. Apply the school behaviour system consistently and keep the response focused on the action that needs to change.
tips: Describe and direct. Name the observable behaviour and the required action, avoiding questions that invite an argument.
Allow take-up time. Give a clear direction, move attention away where appropriate, and return to check compliance.
Use partial agreement carefully. Acknowledge a point without abandoning the expectation: “Even if you were helping, this is silent work.”
Focus on the primary behaviour. Avoid escalating a minor sigh or facial expression while correcting the disruption, unless the secondary behaviour is serious.
Make praise precise. Positive narration and recognition should identify the useful learning action rather than publicly rank pupils.
script: “You are talking while I am explaining. Stop the conversation and listen to this step. Thank you.”
do: Use brief, predictable language and follow through.
Begin with the least intrusive effective response.
avoid: Debating publicly or reacting emotionally.
Inventing consequences outside the agreed school system.
steps: Describe and direct. State the observable behaviour and the expected action instead of asking a confrontational ‘why’ question.
Use partial agreement. Acknowledge the pupil’s comment without abandoning the expectation: ‘Maybe so—and the instruction still stands.’
Allow take-up time. Give the direction once, move attention back to teaching and return later to check compliance rather than creating a public stand-off.
Focus on primary behaviour. Address what is interrupting learning and, unless serious, avoid escalating a sigh, mutter or eye-roll that follows the correction.
Offer directed choices. Give two acceptable, behaviour-based options, state the consequence calmly and follow through consistently.
example: During silent practice, one pupil starts a conversation. The teacher gives a brief description and direction, allows take-up time and resumes monitoring. A quiet return checks that the pupil has begun the task. When another pupil starts promptly, the teacher recognises the specific action. The correction does not become a public debate.

title: Exit routines: ending lessons calmly and efficiently
intro: Use the agreed BSCS exit sequence to finish learning, restore the room and move students calmly into the corridor. Plan sufficient time for practical equipment and resource return.
tips: End the learning deliberately. Do not let premature packing swallow the final explanation or response.
Front-load each action. Tell students what to do before mentioning an object likely to trigger movement.
Use one release cue. Students should know when to act and when to wait.
Check the room before dismissal. Resource return, workspaces, uniform and equipment need a planned check.
Keep sight of the corridor. Dismiss from the threshold in a sequence that allows you to monitor both spaces.
script: “When I say go, pass the books to the end of your row and then wait. Go. Thank you. Now pack away and stand behind your chair.”
do: Use the agreed sequence and concise instructions.
Include room-specific safety and equipment steps.
avoid: Allowing the bell to become the dismissal cue.
Giving several competing packing instructions at once.
steps: Stop the academic activity. Secure attention while enough time remains to complete the room’s exit routine.
Explain resource return. Give one clear instruction and check listening before releasing students to act.
Pack in stages. Cue the remaining actions, including resetting equipment and standing ready; keep students who have finished waiting calmly.
Check readiness. Scan the room, correct unfinished actions and move to the threshold before dismissal.
Dismiss deliberately. Release by the agreed row or group sequence, monitor corridor movement and leave the teaching space ready for the next lesson.
example: At the end of a practical lesson, the teacher finishes the learning before giving the equipment instructions. Pupils return materials on a clear cue, reset the benches and wait ready. After checking safety and room condition, the teacher dismisses by the agreed sequence from the threshold, maintaining a view of the corridor.

title: Do Now: preparing students for learning
intro: At BSCS, Do Now provides a short, independent start using spaced retrieval of previously taught, curriculum-critical knowledge. Keep the routine stable so thinking begins without a fresh explanation.
tips: Use four core questions and a challenge. An accessible first item helps everyone start; later items increase the demand without blocking all progress.
Make answers quick to inspect. A bounded response reveals more than an overloaded question with several unrelated demands.
Teach a stuck protocol. Students move to another item and return, rather than waiting with no work completed.
Make two purposeful laps. First secure participation and the routine; then inspect knowledge and likely errors.
Place prerequisites correctly. Check knowledge required for today’s new content at the opening of Explain, rather than replacing spaced retrieval with a starter on today’s topic.
script: “Complete the four core questions silently, without notes. If you are stuck, move on and return. The final question is an optional challenge.”
do: Protect independent attempts before feedback.
Use a timer and proportionate review.
avoid: Retrieving content students have not yet been taught.
Turning the Do Now into a long worksheet or lengthy reteaching lesson.
steps: Select curriculum-critical knowledge. Use a spaced retrieval plan across recent and older content. Avoid trivia, isolated detail and one-off quiz questions.
Pitch for productive success. Aim for roughly three quarters correct overall: question 1 accessible, questions 2–3 secure for most, question 4 more challenging, plus an optional challenge.

Use clear, single-answer prompts. Prefer discrete facts, features, vocabulary, short procedures or carefully bounded explanations. Do not stack recall, explanation and application into one overloaded prompt.
Make the routine automatic. Display the task in the same place, use a visible timer, keep the response location consistent, and expect quiet independent thinking without notes.
Collect representative evidence. Use mini-whiteboards, Book-to-Board, ABCD cards, call and response or planned indicator pupils rather than volunteers alone.
Respond and reschedule. Correct misconceptions, model briefly where needed, use a related recheck, and return to fragile knowledge in a later Do Now.
example: A Languages Do Now retrieves vocabulary from several earlier lessons, with an accessible first item and an optional translation challenge. Students begin independently without notes. The first teacher lap checks the routine and the second samples answers. A shared vocabulary gap gets a brief repair and is scheduled for retrieval again later.

title: Retrieval practice: strengthening recall
intro: Use retrieval practice to strengthen access to previously taught knowledge. Students should attempt to generate the answer from memory before they see notes, prompts or the solution.
tips: Match retrieval to the knowledge. Use definitions, explanations, diagrams, short procedures and comparisons where each rehearses the intended content.
Teach before testing recall. Repeated failure on untaught or poorly understood material will not repair the original explanation.
Keep the attempt low stakes. Errors reveal what to revisit; avoid creating anxiety through public rankings.
Show useful feedback. Include the reasoning or worked steps where a final answer alone would leave the error unresolved.
Use later retrieval. A correct answer immediately after teaching does not establish durable recall.
script: “Try from memory first. Leave your notes closed. Afterwards we will compare with the model and identify which parts need another retrieval attempt.”
do: Require an independent attempt before revealing answers.
Revisit important gaps after feedback.
avoid: Replacing retrieval with rereading.
Counting copied corrections as successful recall.
steps: Select important taught knowledge. Identify the facts, relationships or process steps students need to retain, and write prompts that retrieve them directly.
Choose the delay. Revisit recent and older learning so recall involves some effort while remaining achievable.
Protect generation. Set a silent independent attempt, keeping solutions hidden and controlling when prompts become available.
Give corrective feedback. Compare answers with an accurate model, repair misunderstandings and let students attempt a related item.
Schedule the return. Bring fragile knowledge back in later lessons, quizzes or homework, varying the cue while keeping the learning focus clear.
example: After teaching photosynthesis, a Biology teacher later asks pupils to reconstruct the word equation from memory. Students attempt before the model appears. Feedback clarifies a common confusion between a reactant and product. A later question uses a different cue so pupils retrieve the relationship again rather than remember the position of words on a slide.

title: Spaced retrieval: revisiting knowledge over time
intro: Use spaced retrieval when students can answer soon after teaching but struggle weeks later. Plan repeated returns to important knowledge rather than treating a topic as finished.
tips: Space the learning, not just the timetable. A later prompt should require students to recall the idea again; displaying the answer beforehand removes that opportunity.
Expect effort. Some forgetting makes retrieval demanding, but repeated near-total failure suggests the delay or prompt needs adjusting.
Keep a curriculum record. Track what has been retrieved and which ideas need another return so selection is deliberate.
Combine spacing with feedback. Correct errors before the next attempt; do not repeatedly rehearse the same wrong answer.
Distinguish spacing from interleaving. Spacing concerns time between encounters; interleaving concerns mixing problem types that require selection.
script: “This question returns to a topic from three weeks ago. Try it from memory before using the worked solution.”
do: Plan returns across lessons and units.
Include both recent and older important knowledge.
avoid: Leaving all revision until the end of a unit.
Assuming one delayed quiz is sufficient for every student.
steps: Identify the durable knowledge. Select the curriculum content students will need to use again, especially prerequisites for later topics.
Map return points. Include an initial practice opportunity and later retrieval across lessons, quizzes and homework.
Vary the cues carefully. Ask for the same knowledge through a definition, example, diagram or application without suddenly testing untaught content.
Respond to forgetting. Explain the important error, provide an accurate model and give another independent retrieval opportunity.
Adjust the next return. Revisit fragile items sooner and maintain occasional retrieval of secure knowledge; do not use a rigid interval regardless of success.
example: An English team maps several returns to important terminology across a unit. Pupils first retrieve definitions, later identify examples and later explain the term in a new text. Incorrect responses receive feedback before another attempt. The returns are spaced across learning rather than concentrated into a single revision lesson before the assessment.

title: Low-stakes quizzes: making retrieval accessible and challenging
intro: Use a recurring low-stakes quiz to revisit knowledge across topics and identify what each student needs to retrieve again. The review matters as much as the score.
tips: Mix recent and older material. Use a deliberate retrieval plan rather than a quiz on whichever questions are easiest to find.
Record confidence before feedback. Confidently held errors can guide the order of review and Review Card creation.
Reveal complete solutions. Students need to see the important decision or method, not merely the final answer.
Keep scores in perspective. The quiz is a learning opportunity; avoid public comparison or turning every attempt into a high-stakes assessment.
Convert errors into retrieval. A corrected script is harder to self-quiz from than a question on the front of a Review Card.
script: “Answer independently. Before we review, rate your confidence. We will begin with important errors and turn those into questions you can practise again.”
do: Protect the independent attempt and feedback sequence.
Plan a later return to corrected knowledge.
avoid: Only testing this week’s content.
Giving a score without explaining the relevant errors.
steps: Plan the content. Select curriculum-critical material across recent and older topics, including short procedures and conceptual distinctions.
Establish the routine. Keep timing, response location and expectations predictable; students attempt without copying or consulting solutions.
Commit before review. Where useful, ask students to rate confidence in each answer before they discover whether it is correct.
Review selectively. Show accurate worked solutions and spend most explanation time on high-value gaps and confidently held errors.
Create future practice. Students make Review Cards or equivalent retrieval prompts, then revisit them in later quizzes, Do Nows or homework.
example: A weekly Maths quiz includes recently practised work and older content. Pupils answer alone and rate confidence before review. The teacher shows worked solutions and spends most time on an important confidently held error. Pupils turn that item into a Review Card and encounter related questions again in later quizzes and homework.

title: Do Now feedback: checking responses and addressing gaps

links.label: Barton - A model for responsive teaching

intro: Use a proportionate review so Do Now both strengthens recall and informs teaching. Gather the answers first, then decide which items need confirmation, discussion or a brief repair.
tips: Do not give every item equal time. A nearly universal correct response rarely needs the same explanation as a common misconception.
Keep the solution hidden while scanning. An early answer changes what later responses can tell you.
Ask for a fresh response after repair. A slightly changed question shows more than asking students to copy the corrected answer.
Use discussion when it has a purpose. Compare different plausible responses, then return to an individual answer so the evidence remains usable.
Record fragile knowledge. Revisit it in future retrieval rather than trying to solve every long-term issue in today’s starter.
script: “Most of us have question one secure, so I will confirm it briefly. Question three shows two different ideas; let us compare those before trying a related question.”
do: Choose the response from the pattern of answers.
Keep the review concise and consequential.
avoid: Asking only volunteers for their answers.
Automatically reteaching every question in full.
steps: Collect independent responses. Use boards, a bounded written answer or a deliberate sample before revealing the solution.
Identify the pattern. Distinguish isolated slips, missing knowledge and a shared misconception; note students whose response remains unclear.
Choose the smallest useful response. Confirm secure items briefly, discuss genuine differences or re-model the point causing widespread difficulty.
Recheck the repaired idea. Use a fresh question with comparable demand and enough change to require independent thinking.
Reschedule the knowledge. Record the item for later retrieval and follow up individual gaps during subsequent teaching or practice.
example: A class answers most Do Now items accurately, but several confuse evaporation with boiling. The teacher confirms secure items briefly, contrasts the two ideas and asks a fresh question about a puddle drying. That response informs the next move. The distinction returns in a later Do Now instead of consuming the entire starter today.

title: Small steps: explaining new ideas in manageable chunks
intro: Use small steps when several interacting decisions make new content hard to follow. Teach a coherent component, rehearse it and then connect it to the next part.
tips: Keep the whole idea visible. Students should know how the current step contributes to the complete process.
Make a step teachable. “Complete question one” is not a learning component; “choose the correct relationship” may be.
Check before adding a dependent step. An error in the first decision can make every later answer misleading.
Use immediate rehearsal. Do not save all student practice until the end of a long explanation.
Recombine deliberately. After components are secure, ask students to complete the process without separate cues for every move.
script: “For this example, we are only choosing the correct equation. Once that decision is secure, we will substitute the values.”
do: Use coherent micro-goals and consistent terminology.
Build back towards independent whole-task performance.
avoid: Fragmenting the content until the overall meaning disappears.
Equating small steps with slow teacher speech.
steps: Set the micro-goal. Signal the one small piece of learning students are about to tackle and link it to prior knowledge.
Model the step. Demonstrate clearly and think aloud so students see what success looks like and why the process works.
Guide immediate practice. Give students a supported attempt straight away using prompts, part-completed examples or peer rehearsal.
Check and correct. Gather responses from all students, diagnose patterns of error and reteach before mistakes become established.
Build to the next step. Move on when most are secure, connect the mastered component to the next and gradually combine steps into a complete process.
example: For a multi-stage calculation, students first choose the relationship, then substitute values, then manage units. The teacher checks each consequential decision before combining the process. Once the separate components are secure, pupils complete a whole calculation with fewer cues. The small steps preserve the overall purpose of the method.

title: The visualiser: live modelling step by step

links.label: DistillED - The Visualiser The Complete Guide

intro: Use the visualiser to show how a response is constructed, including decisions, annotations and revisions. Students see the sequence that a finished example can hide.
tips: Check the back row view. Focus, contrast, orientation and text size matter before the modelling starts.
Rehearse the model. Decide where the difficult choice, likely error and pause will occur; do not improvise the whole process.
Separate watching from copying. When the decision is novel, protect attention to the model and provide recording time afterwards.
Control where students look. Point to the relevant line or feature, and step away from the display when you want attention on you.
Preserve a useful model. Keep it available during early practice, then remove it when students are ready to attempt independently.
script: “Watch this first decision without copying. I am choosing this evidence because it supports the claim. Now pause and identify the feature that made it useful.”
do: Make decisions and revisions visible.
Follow the model with a different guided example.
avoid: Projecting an unreadable polished answer.
Talking continuously while students try to copy every line.
steps: Prepare the surface. Position the visualiser, test the view and lay out the page so key work remains visible without constant movement.
State the goal. Explain what students should attend to and connect the model to the intended learning.
Construct the response. Write, draw or demonstrate one coherent section, narrating the consequential choices rather than every physical action.
Pause deliberately. Check listening, let students read an annotation or ask them to explain a decision before adding complexity.
Move into practice. Give a distinct but related example, keep the model available initially and gather everyone’s first attempt before releasing longer work.
example: A Product Design teacher sketches a joint under the visualiser, narrating why each feature is positioned. Students watch the unfamiliar construction first, then annotate an available model. Their guided task uses a different set of dimensions. The visualiser makes the drawing sequence and decisions visible without turning the lesson into simultaneous copying.

title: Think aloud: making expert thinking visible
intro: Use a think aloud when the important learning sits in the choices an expert makes. Show how you plan, monitor and evaluate, including why you reject an attractive alternative.
tips: Script the consequential decisions. Identify a few places where your reasoning adds value, rather than narrating every movement.
Model monitoring. Show how you notice an implausible answer or a weak sentence and decide what to check.
Explain a rejected option. Students often need to hear why a familiar approach does not fit this task.
Make the thinking transferable. Name the clue, rule or criterion students can use on another example.
Hand over the self-talk. During guided practice, ask students to articulate the same planning or checking move in their own words.
script: “My first thought is to use this quotation, but it describes the setting. I need evidence about the character’s motive, so I will choose this line instead.”
do: Narrate planning, checking and revision.
Keep the model focused on the learning decision.
avoid: A stream of unrelated inner commentary.
Pretending every expert decision is immediate and certain.
steps: Clarify the task. Read the demand and state the goal before starting.
Connect to prior knowledge. Identify a similar task, concept or strategy and explain the link.
Plan and predict. State the intended approach and anticipate where difficulty or error may occur.
Verbalise reasoning. Explain why each decision or method is chosen.
Monitor and adjust. Pause, notice when something looks wrong, check and troubleshoot visibly.
Reflect and evaluate. Summarise what worked, what could improve and what to do next time.
example: An English teacher models selecting evidence. The think aloud explains why an attractive quotation does not support this particular claim, then identifies a better one. During guided practice, pupils name the feature that makes their own quotation relevant. The model reveals a decision they can reuse rather than just the chosen sentence.

title: Examples and non-examples: clarifying what counts
intro: Use examples and non-examples to make the defining feature of a concept clear. Carefully chosen near-misses help students stop relying on superficial appearance.
tips: Choose close contrasts. A near-miss should share enough features with the example to make the boundary worth thinking about.
Change one important feature. Too many simultaneous changes make it difficult to see what determines membership.
Include unusual valid cases. Prevent students from treating the first familiar example as the definition.
Ask for the criterion. “It looks right” is less revealing than a reason linked to the critical feature.
Return to the definition. After comparisons, students should be able to describe what counts and test a new case against it.
script: “Both diagrams look similar. Which is a circuit, and which feature decides? Explain the smallest change that would make the other one a valid example.”
do: Use boundary cases and independent decisions.
Connect the judgement to the defining feature.
avoid: Obviously irrelevant wrong examples.
Changing several features so the critical contrast disappears.
steps: Identify the critical feature. Name the single feature that determines whether something belongs to the concept.
Choose a near-miss. Use a non-example that shares the example’s surface features but removes the critical feature. Avoid random or obviously wrong cases.
Alternate and vary. Show an example, then a related non-example; change one feature at a time so the contrast is visible.
Include boundary cases. Use cases that are just inside or just outside the concept so students must apply the definition, not guess from appearance.
Pause, commit, reveal. Ask what changed and what stayed the same; have every student decide before revealing and explaining the answer.
example: A Maths teacher contrasts a valid rectangle with a near-miss that shares several visual features. Pupils identify the defining properties rather than rely on familiar orientation. A tilted valid example and a plausible invalid case follow. Students justify each classification, making the concept boundary clearer than a page of identical conventional examples.

title: Dual coding: using diagrams and words together
intro: Use words and visuals together when a diagram makes a relationship, sequence or structure easier to understand. Select the representation for its explanatory purpose.
tips: Use a meaningful visual. A diagram should explain the content rather than decorate the slide.
Put labels near their referent. Students should not have to search between a distant key and the relevant feature.
Build gradually. Reveal a structure in the same order as the explanation so attention follows the intended sequence.
Avoid competing language. Pause narration while students read substantial new text.
Ask students to use the representation. Labelling, tracing, explaining and recreating reveal more than simply copying the picture.
script: “Follow this arrow as I explain the transfer. Now describe what it represents. Which part of the diagram shows where the energy is stored?”
do: Align speech, pointing and the displayed feature.
Remove visuals that add no explanatory value.
avoid: Using decorative pictures as evidence of dual coding.
Crowding the diagram with every possible label at once.
steps: Choose the relationship. Decide what the visual will make clearer: position, sequence, cause, comparison or structure.
Design the representation. Use simple shapes, consistent conventions and labels placed close to the relevant features.
Explain in stages. Point or trace while introducing each important part, keeping spoken language aligned with the visual.
Allow processing. Pause for reading, annotation or a short explanation; do not introduce another demand while students inspect new information.
Rehearse the meaning. Ask students to interpret or reconstruct the visual and explain the relationship in words before using it in a new task.
example: In Science, a simple circuit diagram appears in stages as the teacher traces the route. Labels are placed beside components and reading time is separated from narration. Pupils then explain what a connection represents and complete a missing part. The diagram carries the relationship; decorative images would add no useful information.

title: Explicit vocabulary teaching: developing keystone vocabulary

links.label: Tips for Teachers - Alex Quigley on keystone vocabulary

intro: Use explicit vocabulary teaching when disciplinary language is essential to understanding and expressing an idea. Students need to hear, say, use and revisit the word in context.
tips: Select keystone vocabulary. Prioritise words that unlock the current concept and recur in later learning.
Address familiar meanings. Words such as “work”, “power” and “significant” can have a different disciplinary meaning.
Use morphology when useful. A prefix or root can support meaning, but it should not replace the subject definition.
Require use in a full idea. Correct pronunciation alone does not show that a student understands the term.
Revisit through varied cues. Ask for a definition, an example, a non-example or an explanation using the word.
script: “In science, work means energy transferred when a force moves an object. Use that definition to explain which of these examples counts as work.”
do: Teach a precise meaning and examples.
Build repeated use into explanation and practice.
avoid: Giving a long list of definitions to copy once.
Accepting the correct word in an otherwise inaccurate explanation.
steps: Identify the essential term. Choose vocabulary needed to understand the content or produce a precise response.
Say and explain it. Model pronunciation, give a concise definition and connect it to a familiar idea without distorting the meaning.
Show boundaries. Use examples, non-examples and any important contrast with the everyday meaning.
Rehearse active use. Students say, write and apply the term in a sentence, explanation or comparison; prompt precision where necessary.
Return later. Include the term in retrieval and new contexts so students can recognise and use it without the original prompt.
example: In Business Studies, pupils learn the disciplinary meaning of profit and contrast it with revenue. They use the terms in a short explanation and classify examples before calculating. Later retrieval asks for the distinction through a new scenario. Correct use depends on meaning rather than recognising a copied definition.

title: I Do We Do You Do: moving towards independence
intro: Use I Do, We Do, You Do to move students from observing a clear model to accurate independence. The phases may repeat; readiness determines the handover.
tips: Use different examples. We Do should require the same underlying learning without being a copy of the I Do.
Keep the model visible initially. Support comparison without allowing students simply to substitute a superficial detail.
Make We Do genuinely participatory. Every student attempts a step; a few pupils supplying answers is not class-wide rehearsal.
Release a short first task. Inspect early independent work before students repeat the method across many items.
Loop back when needed. Re-model a sticking point rather than persisting with independent work students cannot yet complete.
script: “Watch my example first. You will now try a different example one step at a time. Once those decisions are secure, you will complete the next one independently.”
do: Use evidence to decide the release.
Preserve the connection between model and practice.
avoid: Treating phases as fixed time slots.
Making You Do substantially harder without teaching the new demand.
steps: I Do the model. Explain one coherent example, revealing the method and the reasons for key choices.
We Do a related example. Students supply a decision or step while the teacher guides, checks and corrects.
Check the whole class. Use boards, a brief written response or a practical demonstration rather than assuming readiness from volunteers.
You Do a small attempt. Give a closely matched task that students complete independently, with success criteria and any necessary temporary support.
Increase responsibility. Remove prompts and add variation when performance is sufficiently secure; return to guidance if common errors persist.
example: A teacher models one paragraph, guides a second response using different evidence and collects everyone’s opening claim. Where the claim is secure, pupils attempt another paragraph independently. A common gap in the explanation leads to a short return to modelling. The phases repeat according to readiness rather than a fixed allocation of minutes.

title: Guided practice: checking readiness for independent work
intro: Use guided practice when students have seen an explanation but are not yet ready to perform independently. Keep the demand closely aligned with the model and inspect each important decision.
tips: Use a separate example. Students should apply the model, rather than reproduce the answer they just watched.
Check one step at a time. A final answer can hide where the reasoning broke down.
Keep everyone active. Brief board responses, written steps or rehearsed explanations make the rehearsal class-wide.
Explain why the step works. Correct performance and understanding of the principle both matter.
Extend guidance when necessary. Independence is the destination, but the release should follow sufficient accuracy rather than elapsed minutes.
script: “Try only the first decision. Show me which relationship you will use and why. We will check that before moving to the calculation.”
do: Rehearse the target learning with immediate feedback.
Release responsibility progressively.
avoid: Co-working solely with the most confident pupils.
Leaving students to practise a common error repeatedly.
steps: Frame the rehearsal. Explain that this is supported practice, not a test. Name the specific feature or step being rehearsed and keep the first burst short.
Model and co-work. Show the process briefly, then complete a closely matched example with pupils supplying decisions or steps.
Prompt student explanation. Ask pupils to explain why a step is valid, how it connects to the goal, or what would happen if it changed.
Use all-in practice. Require every pupil to respond through mini-whiteboards, paired explanation, call and response, a short written step or another visible routine.
Give immediate feedback. Name the precise success or misconception, model the correction if needed, and have pupils make the change straight away.
Release gradually. Move from teacher model to co-work, prompted attempt, lightly supported attempt and then a small number of independent items.
example: In Languages, the teacher models a sentence and guides a new one with different vocabulary. Everyone writes the first verb choice before the class continues. A mistaken tense is repaired immediately. Students then complete a short independent set, so the handover follows visible success rather than the contribution of a few fluent speakers.

title: Completion problems: bridging modelling and independence
intro: Use completion problems to bridge a full worked example and an independent solution. Keep part of the successful structure visible while students supply the missing decisions.
tips: Start with the final step. Backward fading keeps the earlier structure available while students finish the process.
Keep demand comparable. Do not remove support and introduce a new representation or harder content in the same move.
Make the blank meaningful. A missing decision reveals more than an obvious word copied from the line above.
Ask for the principle. Students should explain why their completion fits the method or criterion.
Finish with a clean attempt. A complete independent example checks whether the visible structure was doing too much of the work.
script: “The first three steps are complete. Finish the conclusion and explain how the evidence above supports it. On the next example, you will supply the final two steps.”
do: Increase responsibility in manageable stages.
Keep the underlying task stable while fading.
avoid: Removing random lines without a rationale.
Filling blanks that require no meaningful decision.
steps: Model the full example. Complete the method from start to finish and explain the purpose of each important decision.
Fade the final step. Leave only the ending incomplete and ask pupils to finish it while the earlier structure remains visible.
Prompt the principle. Ask pupils to explain the rule, relationship or criterion that makes their completion valid.
Increase the blanks. Remove more of the example so pupils complete progressively larger and earlier sections.
Release a similar task. Pupils plan and complete a closely matched example without the support, then check against the success criteria.
example: A Maths completion task supplies the setup and first lines but leaves the final decision blank. Pupils finish and explain the rule they used. The next task removes the final two stages while keeping the demand comparable. A clean independent question follows, checking whether pupils can organise the method without the visible structure.

title: Fading scaffolds: removing support as students become secure

links.label: DistillED - Provide Scaffolds for Difficult Tasks

intro: Use fading to move students beyond dependence on prompts, models or frames. Decide which support to remove from evidence of what students can now do.
tips: Separate support from difficulty. Keep content familiar while removing a cue, then introduce variation once independence is secure.
Fade a specific feature. Remove the sentence opening, checklist item or worked step that the student no longer needs.
Watch for hidden dependence. Successful copying from a visible model does not establish that the student can choose the approach alone.
Restore the minimum cue. If success drops, reinstate the smallest support that repairs the barrier.
Include later independence. Return after a delay so the task is not supported by immediate memory of the model.
script: “You no longer need the sentence opening. Keep the evidence checklist for this attempt; next time we will try without that too.”
do: Make the withdrawal staged and purposeful.
Check the decisions students make without prompts.
avoid: Keeping a frame permanently for every task.
Removing all support on the same date for every student.
steps: Identify the remaining dependency. Observe which part of the task still requires the model, cue or teacher prompt.
Select the next reduction. Remove one support that successful performance suggests is no longer needed.
Give a comparable attempt. Hold the task demand steady so you can interpret the effect of the reduction.
Respond to the attempt. Keep, reduce or briefly restore a specific cue according to accuracy and reasoning.
Hand over the process. Students plan and complete the task independently, then revisit it later and in a varied context.
example: For an extended response, the teacher first removes the sentence starters but keeps the evidence checklist. After pupils can explain the links independently, the checklist is reduced too. When one student loses the structure, only the necessary cue returns. Support changes with the observed barrier rather than disappearing for the whole class at once.

title: Fluency practice: securing the essential steps

links.label: DistillED - Require and Monitor Independent Practice

intro: Use fluency practice when students understand a process but perform it slowly or inconsistently. Secure accuracy before increasing pace, volume or complexity.
tips: Practise the bottleneck. A short set on the difficult component may be more useful than repeatedly completing the whole task.
Keep correct models available initially. Students should not spend the practice interval repeatedly rehearsing an error.
Increase speed cautiously. Fluency includes accurate, efficient performance; rushing alone is not the aim.
Use purposeful variation. Vary features that require attention while keeping the target skill stable.
Include delayed practice. Smooth performance immediately after modelling can fade unless revisited.
script: “For these six items, practise selecting the correct operation. Accuracy comes first. After that decision is secure, we will complete the full problems.”
do: Monitor early items and correct promptly.
Build towards accurate independent performance.
avoid: Timed competition before the method is secure.
Repeating identical items without attending to their structure.
steps: Identify the component. Locate the decision or action that is accurate but hesitant, or repeatedly disrupts the whole task.
Set a short focused practice set. Keep the target clear and begin with familiar forms.
Inspect early attempts. Correct the faulty step before it is repeated and provide a small prompt or model where needed.
Increase efficiency. Reduce prompts and encourage smoother execution while preserving accuracy and explanation.
Recombine and revisit. Use the component in a complete task, then return after a delay and introduce useful variation.
example: In Music, students practise a short rhythmic component that interrupts a longer performance. The teacher first secures accuracy, then smoother execution and finally recombination with the full phrase. Later rehearsal revisits the same component. Faster playing is useful only when it preserves the timing and technique being practised.

title: Variation: changing examples to deepen understanding
intro: Use variation to help students notice the structure of an idea rather than copy surface features. Decide what changes, what stays the same and why that comparison matters.
tips: Change deliberately. A sequence is not purposeful variation simply because every question looks different.
Include an unchanged relationship. Students need something stable against which to notice the new feature.
Ask for a prediction. Before calculation or completion, ask what they expect to change and why.
Use near-misses. A small change that makes a case invalid can clarify a concept boundary.
Compare after solving. Ask students to explain the effect of the change rather than moving straight to another item.
script: “Only the direction of the arrow has changed. Predict what that changes in the explanation, and identify what remains true.”
do: Select changes that reveal the target relationship.
Ask students to describe the invariant.
avoid: Changing several unfamiliar features at once.
Assuming a varied worksheet automatically produces conceptual understanding.
steps: Choose the relationship. Identify the feature, rule or structure students should notice across examples.
Establish a baseline. Solve or explain one accessible example so the comparison has a clear starting point.
Change a consequential feature. Keep other demands stable and ask students to predict the effect.
Compare the outcomes. Discuss what changed and what remained valid, using the underlying principle rather than appearance.
Test the generalisation. Present a less familiar case and ask students to justify whether the same relationship still applies.
example: A Science teacher changes one condition in a familiar investigation and asks pupils to predict the consequence before calculating or explaining. Pupils compare the new outcome with the baseline and identify the relationship that remains true. A further example tests the generalisation, so variation directs attention to structure rather than mere novelty.

title: Interleaving: practising how to choose an approach
intro: Use interleaving when students can perform several approaches separately but need practice deciding which one fits. Mix types that require a meaningful choice after initial teaching.
tips: Teach each approach first. Interleaving should not disguise missing instruction as desirable difficulty.
Remove the topic label. A heading such as “Use this formula” can supply the decision you want students to practise.
Ask for classification before execution. Students can state the approach and the clue that makes it suitable before completing the task.
Mix related alternatives. Contrast methods students might plausibly confuse, rather than assembling a random set.
Expect performance to feel harder. Inspect the nature of errors and provide feedback; difficulty alone is not evidence the sequence is effective.
script: “These questions need different methods. Before calculating, name the method you would choose and the feature in the question that tells you.”
do: Practise selection as well as execution.
Keep the approaches individually accessible.
avoid: Mixing untaught content into independent practice.
Giving a method cue above every item.
steps: Check initial competence. Confirm that students can use each approach in a familiar form with reasonable accuracy.
Select contrasting types. Choose tasks for which students must discriminate between related methods or concepts.
Mix the sequence. Avoid blocks that reveal which method comes next, while keeping demands manageable.
Require the choice. Ask students to identify the approach and explain the clue before or alongside completing the response.
Give comparative feedback. Address why an alternative did not fit, then revisit the choice in later mixed practice.
example: A Maths practice set mixes tasks requiring different familiar methods. Pupils identify the method and the clue before solving. Feedback compares a plausible alternative with the chosen approach. The difficulty lies partly in selection, whereas a worksheet labelled with one method would have supplied that decision before the pupil began.

title: Independent practice: helping students begin and sustain effort

links.label: DistillED - Require and Monitor Independent Practice

intro: Use independent practice to build accurate, sustained performance after explanation and guided rehearsal. Plan the launch, first items and monitoring so students remain thinking throughout.
tips: Protect the first moments. A brief Golden Silence establishes the expectation before circulation begins.
Teach what to do when stuck. Students can check the model, identify the uncertain step or move to a permitted item; repeated hand-up waiting reduces participation.
Inspect the first attempt. Early diagnosis prevents a whole page of repeated errors.
Provide a meaningful finish task. Deepen the same learning through explanation or variation rather than unrelated extra work.
Preserve productive time. Interrupt only when a common issue makes the class pause worthwhile.
script: “Begin with the first two items independently. If stuck, identify the step that is unclear and use the model. When finished, explain why your method works.”
do: Check readiness before release.
Use a route that includes the whole room.
avoid: Hiding new learning inside the independent task.
Equating a quiet classroom with sustained thinking.
steps: Prepare for success. Use evidence from guided practice to confirm that most pupils can complete the process accurately and identify who still needs a scaffold or teacher check.
Rehearse before release. Correct common misconceptions, make the success criteria visible and clarify what pupils should do if they become stuck.
Mirror before you leap. Begin with the same method, representation and type of material used in guided practice. Do not hide new knowledge inside an 'independent' task.
Monitor in motion. Circulate from the first item, sample the whole room and intervene before an error is repeated across the set.
Build fluency through repetition. Secure accuracy first, then reduce hesitation, increase volume or add carefully selected variation.
Connect to future retrieval. Return to the learning after a delay and mix it with related content so performance becomes durable and flexible.
example: A teacher begins independent practice with two familiar items, clear success criteria and a taught stuck protocol. A short observation establishes the working norm before circulation. Early answers reveal one shared error, so the class receives a bounded repair. Pupils then return to productive practice with a meaningful explanation task for early finishers.

title: Wait time: giving everyone time to think
intro: Use wait time to give everyone a chance to retrieve, reason and prepare an answer. Include a pause after a student response before immediately evaluating or asking someone else.
tips: Match the pause to the question. A complex explanation requires more preparation than a brief factual response; no single number fits every prompt.
Keep the name until after thinking. Naming a pupil first can signal that others need not prepare.
Avoid filling the silence. Rephrasing continuously interrupts the thinking you intended to protect.
Use a jot where useful. A short written commitment gives students a stable starting point for a longer response.
Preserve the second pause. After an answer, allow others to consider it before asking for agreement, challenge or refinement.
script: “Everyone think silently about which source is more reliable. I will give you time before asking for an answer. Prepare the reason as well as your choice.”
do: Make protected thinking time predictable.
Keep every student accountable for the prompt.
avoid: Treating the fastest answer as the best answer.
Announcing thinking time and immediately supplying a hint.
steps: Plan a space-worthy prompt. Use a question that needs retrieval, explanation, justification or evaluation; the required pause should match its complexity.
Set the expectation. Explain that everyone will think before anyone answers and that jotting may be used when the response has several parts.
Wait Time 1: pause after the question. Ask the complete question, then silently count at least three to five seconds—or longer—without rephrasing, filling the silence or signalling a respondent.
Sample an answer. Cold call or use the planned response routine so the protected thinking time belongs to the whole class, not only volunteers.
Wait Time 2: pause after the response. Let the answer land before evaluating it; give peers time to process, then invite elaboration, a build or a challenge.
example: After asking pupils which source better supports a judgement, the teacher gives silent preparation time before naming a respondent. After the answer, another pause allows the class to consider the evidence. A second pupil then compares the reasoning. The question gives more students access than an immediate request for the quickest raised hand.

title: Cold calling: involving everyone in questioning
intro: Use cold calling to make classroom questions an invitation for everyone to think. Build a warm, predictable question–pause–name routine and use answers to guide teaching.
tips: Front-load the response mode. Tell students to think without calling out before posing the question.
Ask before naming. Everyone prepares, then you select the respondent.
Use preparation strategically. Silent thinking, a jot or partner rehearsal helps students develop a response before public contribution.
Distribute questions deliberately. Sample across the room, avoiding repeated reliance on confident pupils or random selection without a purpose.
Respond to uncertainty constructively. Prompt, provide rehearsal or a Second Chance; do not turn a difficult answer into public punishment.
script: “Without hands up or calling out, everyone think: which evidence supports that claim? [Pause.] Priya, what did you choose and why?”
do: Keep the routine predictable and supportive.
Ask follow-up questions about the reasoning.
avoid: Using a question as a sanction for talking.
Naming a pupil before others have had time to think.
steps: Establish the rationale and norms. Explain that everyone thinks, the teacher selects and uncertainty is a normal starting point—not a public trap.
Ask the whole class. Pose a clear factual, conceptual or reasoning question before naming a pupil.
Protect wait time. Allow at least several seconds, and longer for complex prompts; scan the room while everyone prepares.
Invite warmly. Name the pupil with open, supportive language and listen without interrupting the first attempt.
Probe or connect. Ask for evidence, a clearer term, a connection or another pupil’s build; require the class to listen.
Support successful re-entry. Use paired or written rehearsal, pre-call, a prompt, a second pupil’s answer and a return to the original pupil when confidence or knowledge is fragile.
example: A teacher asks everyone to consider why a line of code fails, pauses, then names a pupil. An incomplete response receives a targeted clue and preparation time before the teacher returns. The routine keeps the public answer supportive while requiring everyone to think; it is not used to catch out a pupil who was distracted.

title: Think Pair Share: preparing everyone to answer
intro: Use Think–Pair–Share when students need independent thinking and private rehearsal before a public response. Protect the Think stage so the quickest speaker does not supply everyone’s first idea.
tips: Make thinking silent. Ask for a mental answer or short jot before anyone turns to a partner.
Choose a worthwhile prompt. Explanation, comparison and justification give partners something to develop.
Specify the first speaker. A simple A/B or seating rule prevents negotiation and domination.
Give the listener a task. Restate, question or identify the strongest reason rather than wait for a turn.
Share through accountable sampling. Cold call or collect a fresh individual response; do not assume hearing lively talk means everyone understood.
script: “Think alone and write one reason. Partner A explains first; Partner B checks the evidence. Swap, then be ready to share your partner’s strongest point.”
do: Keep all three stages distinct.
Require both partners to contribute.
avoid: Starting the conversation before individual thinking.
Allowing the Share stage to return to volunteers only.
steps: Design a thinking-worthy prompt. Ask pupils to retrieve, connect, compare, justify or explain; keep the prompt visible as an anchor.
Protect THINK. Give uninterrupted silent time for each pupil to retrieve and, when useful, jot keywords, evidence or a first decision.
Structure PAIR. Specify who speaks first, what the listener must do, when roles swap and what the pair must improve or agree.
Run an inclusive SHARE. Cold call pairs or individuals so either partner may summarise, justify or report the other person’s idea; probe contrasting reasoning.
Adapt the sequence. Use Think–Write–Pair–Share, partner-summary writing, mini-whiteboards or a batched share when these strengthen retrieval or accountability.
example: In Geography, pupils individually choose the most important cause and write a reason. Partners compare evidence with clear speaking roles, then pupils share a partner’s strongest point. A final individual explanation captures the refined thinking. The initial silent stage prevents one confident partner supplying both pupils’ starting ideas.

title: Turn and Talk: structuring purposeful partner discussion
intro: Use Turn and Talk for a short, purposeful exchange that helps students clarify or rehearse an idea. Specify the question, partner roles, time and response you will collect afterwards.
tips: Prime the end as well as the start. Students should know how they will stop and what answer they must be ready to give.
Stop at the crest of the wave. End while useful exchange is active rather than waiting until every pair has exhausted the prompt.
Listen for the thinking. Sample the content of talk, not merely whether pupils are speaking.
Ask about the partner. A request to restate the other person’s reasoning creates listening accountability.
Re-vote individually where appropriate. After comparing ideas, students commit again so you can see changed thinking.
script: “Partner A explains which option fits; Partner B challenges the reason. Swap after thirty seconds. Afterwards I may ask you to explain your partner’s choice.”
do: Set a specific cognitive question and clear roles.
Harvest the discussion deliberately.
avoid: “Discuss this” with no product or purpose.
Letting one partner deliver both contributions.
steps: Build predictable pairs. Use stable A/B partners where possible and decide the speaking order, including a planned trio when numbers require it.
Give thinking time. Protect five to ten seconds—or longer—so each pupil retrieves, annotates or drafts before speaking.
Structure the question. Ask pupils to explain, justify, compare, predict, evaluate or rank, using content already taught or made available.
Provide a concrete stimulus. Anchor talk in a text, graph, model, image, worked example, data or vocabulary prompt rather than memory-free opinion.
Rehearse briefly and account. Use short bursts, switch speakers explicitly, stop near the crest of productive talk and cold call pupils to share or summarise.
example: In English, paired talk compares two interpretations of a line. Each partner must give a reason and respond to the other. The teacher samples the discussion, signals its end while useful talk is active and asks selected pupils to explain their partner’s reasoning. Students then refine their own written interpretation.

title: Choral response: rehearsing brief answers together
intro: Use choral response for brief, unambiguous answers that benefit from shared rehearsal. Teach a precise cue so students begin together rather than copying the earliest voice.
tips: Choose a bounded response. A key term, short fact or agreed phrase works better than an open explanation.
Build thinking before the cue. Students should know the answer they intend to give before the chorus starts.
Rehearse with easy content. Establish the mechanics separately from challenging subject knowledge.
Listen for accuracy. A loud chorus can hide missing, delayed or incorrect responses.
Use another check for diagnosis. When you need individual evidence, follow with a board response, written answer or targeted sample.
script: “Think first. On ‘everyone in three, two, one’, say the missing word together. Plants take in carbon… Everyone in three, two, one.”
do: Use a consistent, rehearsed response cue.
Keep answers short and precise.
avoid: Treating volume as proof of individual understanding.
Using an ambiguous prompt with several possible responses.
steps: Choose suitable content. Use choral response for a brief fact, phrase, pronunciation, definition or completed step with one clear answer—not an extended explanation.
State and model the routine. Teach the cue, expected volume and complete response; model difficult vocabulary before the class attempts it.
Ask, think, cue. Pose the prompt, allow silent retrieval and give one unambiguous signal so every voice begins together.
Listen for participation and accuracy. Attend to timing, confidence and the content of the response; reset if voices are missing or the response is ragged.
Affirm or correct immediately. Name what was accurate, or provide the correct answer with a brief explanation and have the class repeat it precisely.
Check individuals when needed. Follow with cold call, mini-whiteboards or a process question; a chorus cannot by itself prove each pupil understands.
example: A Languages teacher rehearses a short phrase on a common cue after protected thinking time. The teacher listens for accurate pronunciation and repeats the troublesome part. A later individual written response checks the meaning. The chorus supports shared rehearsal without being treated as evidence that every pupil independently understands the phrase.

title: Probing questions: moving beyond the first answer

links.label: Barton - Plan follow-up questions in advance

intro: Use probing questions after students have relevant knowledge to deepen or clarify the reasoning behind an answer. Plan a focused follow-up rather than asking a vague “Why?” every time.
tips: Probe a consequential decision. Ask which clue, criterion or relationship produced the answer.
Plan likely follow-ups. Prepare a question for an incomplete answer, a misconception and a secure explanation.
