Hold the pupil’s thinking. Give a prompt, then return to the same student to complete the response.
Use precise language. “Which feature ruled out A?” is often clearer than “Tell me more.”
Involve listeners. Ask others to restate, compare or challenge the reasoning before moving on.
script: “You chose the second source. Which feature makes it more trustworthy for this question? What evidence would weaken your judgement?”
do: Anchor the probe to a visible answer or step.
Prompt a fuller disciplinary explanation.
avoid: Asking students to reason about untaught material.
Finishing their answer for them and accepting your own explanation.
steps: Establish the knowledge. Explain or model the method, concept or example before asking pupils to reveal how it works.
Anchor the probe. Begin from a pupil answer, a worked step, a comparison or a decision the class can see.
Ask one focused how or why. Target the clue used, the first step, the reason for a choice, a link to prior knowledge or an error that must be corrected.
Refine and rehearse. Prompt the pupil to add evidence, use precise vocabulary, sequence the explanation or improve it after hearing a peer.
Return to the process. Revisit the reasoning in a related example so the method becomes transferable rather than a one-off performance.
example: A pupil identifies the correct result but offers little reasoning. The teacher asks which feature ruled out the alternative, then asks the pupil to complete the explanation using the key term. Another pupil compares the reasoning with a second case. The follow-up deepens a specific decision instead of becoming a vague extended interrogation.

title: Compare justify evaluate: questions that deepen reasoning

links.label: Barton - Plan follow-up questions in advance

intro: Use comparison, justification and evaluation prompts when students need to explain a relationship or make a judgement. Ensure they have the knowledge and criteria required to reason well.
tips: Make comparison focused. Specify the feature or relationship to compare rather than asking for every possible similarity and difference.
Require evidence. “I prefer this one” becomes useful when linked to a criterion or example.
Choose genuinely comparable cases. If one is obviously poor, the judgement may demand little thought.
Ask for an alternative. Students can explain what would make the other option defensible.
Rehearse before public answers. A written claim and evidence or structured partner exchange can improve the precision of the response.
script: “Compare the two methods for this task. Which is more efficient, and what evidence supports that judgement? When might the other method be preferable?”
do: State the criterion and demand a reason.
Use taught knowledge to support the judgement.
avoid: Vague preferences without disciplinary evidence.
An evaluation task before students know what quality means.
steps: Choose the thinking demand. Decide whether students are identifying a contrast, defending a claim or judging quality against a criterion.
Prepare the cases. Select examples close enough to require attention to the important difference.
State the criteria. Clarify which knowledge, evidence or performance feature should inform the response.
Protect preparation. Give silent time to form a claim and supporting reason, then use talk or writing to refine it.
Probe and transfer. Ask what would change the judgement and test the same criterion in a fresh case.
example: In Art, pupils compare two compositions against a taught criterion. They identify a feature, explain its effect and justify which better meets the purpose. A changed brief then asks whether the judgement would change. The evaluation draws on disciplinary knowledge rather than a preference for whichever work initially looks more attractive.

title: Mini-whiteboards: checking everyone's understanding
intro: Make every student’s answer visible, identify gaps and decide what to teach next. Useful before independent practice or whenever answers from a few students leave you unsure about everyone else.
tips: Separate working from the answer. Use one side for working and the other for a large final answer; turn it over when explaining the method.
Bring bookwork onto boards. Transfer the answer to one pivotal book question onto a board, then scan before showing the solution.
Investigate blank boards. Ask what the student knows or which part is unclear; offer a starting prompt and return.
Control public answers. Avoid praising an early correct board while others are writing; gather the evidence before revealing the solution.
Keep the routine available. Working pens, erasers and boards should be within reach; re-model premature erasing or unreadable answers.
script: “One formula, written large. Keep it hidden. Write the formula for magnesium chloride.” [Thinking time.] “Pens down. Show me in three, two, one. Hold still while I check.”
do: Scan every response before giving the answer.
Probe reasoning and use a fresh check after repair.
avoid: Accepting the first correct board as evidence for everyone.
Using boards to rank students or as punishment.
steps: Plan a revealing question. Target one idea, anticipate plausible wrong answers and choose a word, calculation, sketch or choice that can be scanned.
Rehearse the mechanics. Model clear writing, private answers, boards facing you and erasing only on signal; practise with an easy question.
Secure independent thinking. Give response instructions before the question, allow time and keep boards hidden until commitment is complete.
Collect every response. Reveal together and scan systematically. If revealing back to front, everyone stops writing before the first row shows.
Probe and respond. Look for common errors and missing responses, ask how selected students decided, then Pause & Fix, Adapt & Support or Extend & Challenge as the evidence warrants.
example: Several Chemistry boards show MgCl rather than MgCl₂. The teacher keeps the responses private until all pupils commit, identifies the pattern and re-models charge balance. Pupils then answer a different ionic formula question. Correcting the original board alone would have shown compliance with the model rather than independent application.

title: Hinge questions: deciding whether to move on
intro: Use a hinge question at a decision point where students’ answers should change what happens next. Plan the question and the teaching response together.
tips: Identify the hinge. Choose a concept that students need before the next task or explanation will make sense.
Match each distractor to an error. An option should tell you what needs clarifying, not just whether the answer is wrong.
Collect independent answers first. Discussion can improve learning afterwards, but initial private commitment gives cleaner diagnostic evidence.
Decide your likely responses. Plan what you will do for a common misconception, mixed understanding and broadly secure answers.
Ask a fresh follow-up. The response after repair should require application, not memorisation of the original option.
script: “Choose privately and prepare your reason. We will use the responses to decide whether we are ready for the next example or need to revisit this distinction.”
do: Place the question before a consequential increase in demand.
Inspect reasoning and the pattern of choices.
avoid: A quiz item with no effect on the next teaching move.
Automatically moving on when a fixed percentage is correct.
steps: Plan the hinge in advance. Choose a pivotal concept and build plausible distractors from common misconceptions rather than random errors.
Ask it after a small teaching chunk. Place the question just before the lesson would otherwise move into the next explanation or practice demand.
Protect independent commitment. Give silent thinking time, keep the answer hidden and collect a whole-class response before partner discussion where initial diagnosis matters.
Scan choices and reasoning. Look for patterns, then invite pupils to explain why an option was attractive before revealing the correct answer.
Make the instructional decision. Move on when understanding is sufficiently secure; otherwise re-explain the identified misconception, use a different example or extend guided practice.
Recheck and refine. Test the same concept in a related form and later improve distractors that did not reveal the intended thinking.
example: Before a new stage in a calculation, a hinge question checks the relationship needed for that stage. Each option represents a different likely misconception. Independent choices reveal a shared error, so the teacher pauses, contrasts the methods and asks a fresh question. The planned next task changes because of the evidence.

title: Checking for understanding during explanations

links.label: Barton - Checking for understanding Ten key principles

intro: Use checks during and between explanation chunks to find out what students can recall, distinguish or apply. Gather evidence that informs a specific teaching decision.
tips: Distinguish listening from understanding. Repeating what was said checks receipt; a fresh application checks whether the idea can be used.
Plan five useful checkpoints. Do Now review, prerequisites, basics after explanation, hinges and readiness for independent practice offer different evidence.
Use TAPPLE thoughtfully. Teach, Ask, Pair-share after independent thinking, Pick non-volunteers, Listen, and give Effective feedback.
Preserve independent evidence. Collect an initial answer before partner talk where you need to diagnose each pupil’s starting understanding.
Prepare the response. A check is useful when it helps you decide whether to clarify, practise, support or extend.
script: “First answer alone. Now compare the reasoning with your partner. I will ask for explanations, then everyone will try a new example independently.”
do: Check the specific idea just taught.
Respond and use a fresh related question.
avoid: “Any questions?” as the main evidence.
Treating a correct volunteer answer as class readiness.
steps: Teach it first. Explain or model one coherent step before asking pupils to demonstrate understanding; do not use a cold question to test untaught material.
Ask a specific question. Ask what pupils understand, can distinguish or can do—not whether they understand. Script high-value recall, application, misconception and process prompts in advance.
Pair-share after silent thinking. Give 5–10 seconds to think, then a brief, structured Turn and Talk with labelled partners and an expectation of full-sentence rehearsal.
Pick non-volunteers. Cold call after the rehearsal so everyone remains accountable and the public sample is not limited to confident volunteers.
Listen to the response. Attend to target vocabulary, reasoning and the pattern across responses. Probe incomplete thinking instead of fishing for the answer.

Give effective feedback and act. Echo a secure answer, elaborate tentative thinking, or explain and reteach an error. Aim for about 80% success before moving on, then continue support until everyone can access the next step.
example: After a short explanation, students first answer a new case alone. They compare reasoning in pairs, and the teacher samples non-volunteers before a fresh individual check. Responses show whether the difficulty concerns the principle or a missed instruction. The teacher can then choose a specific repair rather than repeat the whole explanation.

title: Circulation: sampling independent work and responding
intro: Use circulation to read learning across the room, identify the exact error and choose a response. Move with a route and a diagnostic focus rather than following raised hands alone.
tips: Inspect one feature at a time. Look for the first decision, selected evidence or a specific presentation feature so the scan stays purposeful.
Include likely invisible pupils. Deliberately visit students whose work or thinking you do not normally hear.
Visit strong work early too. It helps establish the expected standard and can supply an exemplar for later discussion.
Keep the whole room visible. Step back between individual interactions; avoid becoming absorbed at one desk.
Record patterns briefly. A quick note or seating-plan mark helps distinguish an individual gap from a class-wide issue.
script: “I am checking the reason you chose this method. Show me that decision. Fix this line, then try the next item; I will return shortly.”
do: Use scan, read and compare with the criterion.
Return after a targeted intervention.
avoid: Wandering without a focus.
Explaining at length beside one pupil while losing the rest of the room.
steps: Plan the route. Identify the success criterion, likely errors and pupils you must see, with a path that covers every area.
Observe first attempts. After securing the launch, inspect early work before students repeat the process many times.
Diagnose the response. Read the relevant section and ask a brief question where the reasoning is unclear.
Give a bounded next action. Use a prompt, clue or direct explanation according to need, then require the pupil to do the thinking.
Revisit and decide. Check the change; preserve productive work where gaps are isolated, or pause the class when the pattern justifies reteaching.
example: During essay practice, the teacher’s route checks the claim–evidence link in selected first paragraphs across the room. Quick notes distinguish missing evidence from weak explanation. Some pupils receive an individual prompt; a shared pattern becomes a brief class model. The teacher returns to inspect the changed sentence before continuing the route.

title: Exit tickets: identifying what needs revisiting

links.label: Barton - Diagnostic questions as exit tickets

intro: Use an exit ticket when a brief independent response can inform the next lesson. Choose essential knowledge and a format that can be reviewed quickly.
tips: Keep the ticket narrow. One useful conceptual distinction may reveal more than five broad questions.
Include reasoning where necessary. A letter choice alone can hide why the student selected it.
Protect independence. A ticket copied after class discussion gives less information about the individual’s understanding.
Sort before annotating. Group responses by secure, partly secure and insecure, then inspect the causes of difficulty.
Prepare the next move. Decide whether tomorrow needs retrieval, a brief clarification, guided practice or a fuller reteach.
script: “Before you leave, answer this alone: which example shows diffusion, and which feature tells you? Include one sentence explaining your choice.”
do: Target the learning that matters for the next lesson.
Use the responses to plan teaching.
avoid: Collecting tickets without reviewing them.
A long end-of-lesson assessment with no time to complete it.
steps: Choose the purpose. Identify the essential idea or prerequisite you need to inspect before the next lesson.
Write a short prompt. Use a bounded explanation, diagnostic choice, diagram or small performance that reveals the target knowledge.
Allow an independent response. Reserve enough time and keep the solution hidden until students have committed.
Divide and inspect. Sort by quality of understanding, then look closely at the main error patterns and selected unclear answers.
Decide the next lesson response. Plan a fresh retrieval or diagnostic prompt and the explanation, rehearsal or support the evidence warrants.
example: A Computing exit ticket asks pupils to predict the output of a short, taught code structure and explain one decision. The teacher sorts the answers and finds a common misunderstanding. The next lesson begins with a related check and a short repair, rather than starting new content over an unresolved prerequisite.

title: Pause and Fix: responding to a common misconception

links.label: Barton - A model for responsive teaching

intro: Use Pause & Fix when a common gap means continuing would reinforce an error or make the next step inaccessible. Stop briefly, repair the precise issue and return to a fresh attempt.
tips: Pause for a consequential pattern. A few isolated slips may need individual feedback rather than stopping productive class work.
Change the explanation. Repeating the same long account more loudly rarely addresses the faulty idea.
Keep the repair bounded. State the specific distinction you are fixing and show it with one clear example.
Keep secure students thinking. Ask them to explain the misconception or test a useful variation rather than sit through unnecessary repetition.
Recheck before resuming. Use changed surface details and the same conceptual demand so students must apply the repair.
script: “Pause. Several answers use the mass in place of the volume. We will model that distinction once, then everyone will try a new example.”
do: Match the repair to the shared error.
Secure attention before re-explaining.
avoid: Stopping the class for every interesting error.
Treating copied corrections as proof the issue is fixed.
steps: Identify the common gap. Use responses or work to locate the knowledge or decision causing widespread difficulty.
Stop and frame the repair. Secure attention, name the issue neutrally and explain why this short pause matters.
Re-model differently. Use a smaller step, contrasting example or clearer representation that addresses the error directly.
Give a fresh check. Require every student to apply the idea to a related example before you reveal the answer.
Resume proportionately. Continue when the evidence supports it, with targeted follow-up for remaining gaps; extend the repair when the class is still insecure.
example: In Maths practice, several pupils apply the same invalid cancellation. The teacher stops, identifies the exact condition for a valid move and contrasts the two cases. Everyone then attempts a new item. Once the class pattern is secure, practice resumes with individual follow-up for remaining gaps rather than a complete restart of the topic.

title: Adapt and Support Extend and Challenge: responding to different needs

links.label: Barton - A model for responsive teaching

intro: Use Adapt & Support and Extend & Challenge when responses show different needs. Keep the learning goal ambitious while adjusting the support or depth of the next task.
tips: Diagnose before grouping. The same incorrect answer can come from different barriers; a quick probe may change the support needed.
Use flexible groups. Group briefly by the current learning need, then release students when they can proceed independently.
Extend through depth. Ask for justification, a boundary case or transfer rather than simply more identical questions.
Preserve a common thread. Students should remain working on the intended knowledge even when support differs.
Return to independent evidence. A successful response beside the teacher may depend on prompts; check what the student can do alone.
script: “If you need the first-step prompt, use it for this example. If your method is secure, explain how the answer changes when this condition changes.”
do: Adjust support to the observed barrier.
Provide meaningful challenge for secure students.
avoid: Permanent task assignment by label or prior attainment.
Giving different groups unrelated learning goals.
steps: Read the pattern. Identify which students need a prompt, a re-model or more guided practice and which are ready for deeper application.
Locate the barrier. Check whether the issue concerns knowledge, vocabulary, task structure or a specific decision.
Select the smallest support. Give a useful cue, model, frame or short teacher group while retaining the curricular goal.
Extend the secure learning. Use explanation, variation or a less familiar case that requires additional thinking.
Hand back responsibility. Remove support as competence becomes visible and use independent responses to decide the next adjustment.
example: In Science, some pupils need a prompt to select the relationship while others can justify it independently. A short teacher group rehearses the first decision; secure pupils explore how a changed condition affects the result. All work remains connected to the same concept, and the temporary support is removed when students can proceed alone.

title: Actionable feedback: giving students a useful next step
intro: Use individual feedback when a precise next action can improve work while the thinking is still live. Make the location, learning issue and required change clear.
tips: Begin with the successful feature. Precise recognition tells the pupil what to retain while improving another part.
Use prompt, clue, direct. Start with a question if the pupil has the knowledge; provide more guidance when the response shows it is needed.
Bound the action. One sentence or process step is easier to act on than “improve your explanation”.
Ask for immediate work. A feedback conversation should end with the student thinking, writing, rehearsing or trying again.
Return later. Check the change and an additional attempt rather than assuming the comment was understood.
script: “Your claim is clear. In this sentence, add evidence that supports it. Tell me what you will change, then make the edit and I will return.”
do: Name the exact feature and next action.
Check listening and require a response.
avoid: Vague praise followed by “more detail”.
Giving the answer when a usable prompt would suffice.
steps: Plan and break the plane early. Name the success criteria, must-check pupils and a predictable route before work begins.
Cover the full field. Move systematically, stay aware of the room and avoid reactive zig-zagging or repeatedly visiting the same pupils.
Diagnose before feeding back. Scan, read and compare with the criteria; note exemplars, partial attempts, misconceptions and pupils to revisit.
Use prompt, clue, then direct. Start with the least support likely to activate the pupil's knowledge; escalate only when the response shows it is needed.
Bound the action. Identify the exact location and a finite improvement that the pupil can complete now.
Return and respond. Check the change, praise against criteria and pause for whole-class correction when the same misconception is widespread.
example: In PE, a pupil receives feedback on one feature of a taught movement. The teacher identifies what is already successful, gives a precise next action and asks for another attempt. A later return checks the change. The feedback is short enough to use immediately and does not become a list of every possible improvement.

title: Whole-class feedback: responding to patterns in work
intro: Use whole-class feedback when students’ work reveals shared strengths and recurring difficulties. Review the pattern once, then give everyone a useful improvement task.
tips: Select a small number of high-value issues. Two or three important misconceptions can be more useful than reviewing every mark lost.
Prepare before returning scores. Deliver the model and recheck while attention is on learning rather than individual results.
Use barometer work carefully. Selected work can reveal patterns, but do not assume a small sample captures every need.
Model, recheck, stretch. Use a fresh equivalent question after the explanation, then a useful variation when secure.
Make errors retrievable. Review Cards turn selected individual gaps into future practice, beyond today’s correction.
script: “This feature was secure across many responses. This next error appeared often, so we will model it, try a related question and then improve our own work.”
do: Choose the response from reviewed student work.
Allocate time for students to act.
avoid: A presentation of comments with no improvement task.
Reteaching every error for the same amount of time.
steps: Review student work. Read the relevant body of work to identify common strengths, misconceptions and repeated errors; avoid annotating every piece in detail.
Record key feedback. Use a crib sheet for success criteria, what went well, model answers, misconceptions, key vocabulary, SPaG patterns and next actions.
Plan the response. Choose a model, comparison, live edit, brief reteach, discussion or practice task that will turn the pattern into learning.
Deliver feedback visibly. Use the board, visualiser, screen or handout to show strong examples and typical errors without exposing or embarrassing pupils.
Get pupils thinking and improving. Allocate time for a focused response: redraft, rehearse, revisit, re-learn or research, according to the learning need.
Reflect and respond. Check the improvements, decide what requires future teaching and revisit fragile learning through practice, retrieval or a hinge question.
example: An English assessment reveals a recurring weak explanation after evidence. The teacher selects a model and near-miss, improves the connection live and asks pupils to complete a fresh equivalent paragraph. Work is then returned for an individual improvement task. Feedback becomes instruction and practice rather than repeated comments on many scripts.

title: Self-checking: teaching students to improve their own work
intro: Use self-checking when students know what quality looks like but do not yet inspect their own work reliably. Teach a specific checking action rather than telling them to “check it”.
tips: Teach what to inspect. Specify a claim–evidence link, sign, unit or process decision rather than an unlimited search.
Use a model and a near-miss. Students need to see the feature present and absent before finding it in their own work.
Separate checking from rereading. A purposeful check asks a question of the work and may require recalculation, comparison or evidence tracing.
Give one checking focus first. Build fluency before expecting a long checklist to be used independently.
Check the checker. Sample how students located and repaired the issue; a tick beside a criterion is not evidence of accurate self-assessment.
script: “Underline your claim and circle the evidence. Draw an arrow where the sentence explains how the evidence supports the claim. Which link is missing?”
do: Model the checking process and require a visible action.
Fade prompts as checking becomes reliable.
avoid: “Check your work” with no taught process.
Assuming every self-awarded tick is accurate.
steps: Select the checking focus. Choose a consequential feature students have been taught and can recognise.
Demonstrate the check. Think aloud while inspecting a model and identifying a near-miss.
Rehearse on shared work. Students locate the feature or error in an example before moving to their own response.
Apply and improve. Require a visible checking action and an explained correction, rather than silent rereading alone.
Transfer the routine. Use the same checking question on a fresh task, then reduce the external prompt when students can apply it reliably.
example: In Science, pupils check the units in their calculations using a taught sequence: identify the quantity, inspect the substitution and inspect the final unit. They correct and explain a mismatch, then use the routine on another question. A generic instruction to check the whole page would have provided less guidance about the thinking required.

title: Peer critique: using criteria to improve work
intro: Use peer critique when students understand the content and criteria well enough to offer accurate, useful feedback. Teach the feedback routine before exchanging work.
tips: Use SPARK. Comments should be Specific, Prescriptive, Actionable, Referenced to a criterion and Kind.
Model a weak comment too. Comparing “good work” with a precise suggestion helps students see what usefulness means.
Start with one criterion. Narrow the demand before expecting peers to judge an entire piece.
Keep responsibility with the recipient. Students should evaluate the comment, make a justified change and explain it.
Sample accuracy. Peer feedback does not replace teacher expertise when a misconception is difficult to diagnose.
script: “Identify one success against the criterion. Then pinpoint one place to improve and suggest an action. The writer will decide how to use it and explain the change.”
do: Teach the criteria and model useful comments.
Require the recipient to act.
avoid: Exchanging work before students know the standard.
Personal preferences or vague praise presented as critique.
steps: Establish the culture. Explain that critique is a learning tool and agree the norm: kind, specific and helpful.
Make quality visible. Clarify the criteria and compare model, near-miss and weak feedback comments.
Model SPARK live. Use anonymous work to demonstrate how a precise observation becomes a referenced, actionable suggestion.
Rehearse before exchange. Co-construct comments, evaluate examples and use sentence stems until pupils can distinguish strong from vague feedback.
Give and receive feedback. Begin with a genuine strength, then identify one high-impact improvement connected to the criteria.
Act and close the loop. The recipient decides how to use the comment, revises the work and explains the change; the teacher samples quality and accuracy.
example: In Art, pupils first compare useful and vague critique against one criterion. They then give a precise observation and an actionable suggestion on a partner’s work. The recipient evaluates the suggestion, revises the selected feature and explains the change. The teacher samples whether comments are accurate as well as respectful.

title: Feedback tasks: planning time to act on feedback

links.label: Barton - Correcting in green pen does not work

intro: Use feedback tasks to make improvement an act of thinking. Select a solvable challenge that helps students locate, explain and repair an issue rather than simply copy a correction.
tips: Use detective work when pupils can solve it. Give the number and type of issues, then let students find and fix them.
Add the minimum cue. Narrow to a paragraph, step or criterion if the search is too broad.
Give direct teaching where needed. An error caused by missing knowledge is not a productive puzzle.
Protect action time. Plan redrafting, rehearsal, reattempting or re-testing into the lesson rather than hoping students act later.
Require an explanation. Ask what changed and why, then use a related task where the corrected learning matters.
script: “Two statements misuse the key term. Find them, explain the issue and correct them using the definition and the model.”
do: Set a bounded, achievable improvement action.
Keep pupils doing the cognitive work.
avoid: Cryptic feedback on an error students cannot diagnose.
Colour-coded corrections with no new thinking.
steps: Choose a narrow learning focus. Identify the knowledge, skill or misconception that matters and that pupils can realistically improve.
Record what needs fixing without annotating it. Mark or review the work, then state the number and type of issues rather than correcting each location.
Pose a solvable search. Tell pupils what they are looking for and what success will look like, but leave the locating and correcting to them.
Add the minimum cue if needed. Narrow the section, paragraph, step or error type without revealing the exact line or answer.
Protect in-class time to act. Return the work when pupils have time to search, think, revise and use relevant models or criteria.
Close the loop. Ask pupils to explain what they changed and why, check the correction and later test whether they can apply the learning independently.
example: In Languages, the teacher identifies the number and type of errors in a familiar paragraph without correcting each location. Pupils use the model and criteria to find, explain and repair them. When a pupil lacks the relevant rule, the teacher gives direct teaching rather than leave the student in an unproductive search.

title: Feedback follow-up: checking improvement on a new task

links.label: Barton - Correcting in green pen does not work

intro: Use feedback follow-up to find out whether the learning improved beyond the original correction. A new attempt gives more useful evidence than a rewritten answer alone.
tips: Plan the new item before feedback. This keeps the improvement focus precise and prevents the follow-up becoming an afterthought.
Keep the demand comparable. An unexpectedly harder question makes it difficult to interpret whether the correction helped.
Change enough to require thinking. A clone with one number swapped may reward imitation.
Revisit after a delay. Immediate success can depend on recent memory of the teacher’s explanation.
Inspect the process. A correct final answer may still hide the original faulty reasoning.
script: “You have corrected the worked example. Now close it and try this new case. Explain the decision that prevents the same error.”
do: Use independent application on a fresh task.
Record remaining gaps for later teaching.
avoid: Counting a copied model as improved understanding.
Never returning to the learning after the feedback lesson.
steps: Identify the intended improvement. State the knowledge, decision or feature the feedback should change.
Prepare a related task. Retain the conceptual demand while altering the example enough to require application.
Deliver feedback and action time. Model or prompt the correction and require the student to practise the repaired idea.
Collect an independent attempt. Reduce access to the original solution and inspect both answer and reasoning.
Return after a delay. Use a later retrieval or application task and decide whether further explanation, rehearsal or support is necessary.
example: After feedback on a misconception, pupils try a fresh question with comparable demand and no visible original solution. The teacher inspects the reasoning, not just the final answer. The learning returns in a later quiz. This separates immediate successful correction from the student’s ability to use the repaired idea independently over time.

title: Worked examples: showing a complete solution
intro: Use a worked example when students need to see the full structure of a successful response before attempting a complex task. Make the important decisions and criteria visible.
tips: Choose a representative example. The model should expose the method students need, without an exceptional trick or distracting complexity.
Include the reasoning. A correct sequence with no rationale can encourage superficial copying.
Keep the layout transferable. Use a clear structure students can apply to another response.
Compare with a near-miss. A small error can reveal why the successful step is necessary.
Bridge to completion problems. Remove selected final steps before expecting the whole process independently.
script: “This is a complete answer. Notice the claim, evidence and explanation. We will identify what each part does, then complete a different answer with the final section missing.”
do: Show the complete method and its key decisions.
Move to a distinct related example.
avoid: A polished answer with no explanation of its structure.
Assuming copying the model establishes independent competence.
steps: Clarify the task. State what successful performance looks like and confirm the prerequisites students need.
Present the complete example. Show the response in a clear sequence or structure, with relevant workings and criteria.
Explain consequential choices. Point to where the method, evidence or feature satisfies the task and why an alternative would fail.
Rehearse the structure. Ask students to explain a step, compare a near-miss or complete a partly worked related example.
Hand over the method. Give a fresh independent task and remove the model when students can use the underlying structure without it.
example: A Business Studies worked example shows the complete response structure, calculations and interpretation. The teacher identifies why each part is needed, then contrasts a near-miss. Pupils complete a different example with the final section missing before attempting the whole response independently. The complete model provides a route into the demand.

title: The visualiser: discussing and improving student work

links.label: DistillED - The Visualiser The Complete Guide

intro: Use the visualiser to make student work a shared learning resource. Select a response because it illustrates a useful success, misconception or improvement decision.
tips: Select with a purpose. Decide which feature the class should notice before projecting the work.
Establish a respectful culture. Sharing should feel routine; anonymise where useful and avoid public embarrassment.
Keep the discussion narrow. One paragraph, diagram or process step often produces a clearer learning focus than the whole page.
Show the edit live. Explain why the change improves the response, retaining successful features.
Transfer to students’ own work. Everyone should make an equivalent improvement rather than merely watch the projected edit.
script: “This paragraph gives a clear claim. Let us find where the explanation stops short. We will improve that link, then you will inspect the same feature in your own paragraph.”
do: Make the criterion and revision visible.
Use contrasting responses to clarify quality.
avoid: Displaying work solely to celebrate presentation.
Critiquing a named pupil rather than the response.
steps: Select the response. Choose a useful exemplar or near-miss and identify the learning feature it will reveal.
Prepare the display. Check readability, crop or mask irrelevant details and frame the sharing respectfully.
Ask students to inspect. Give silent time and a specific question about the criterion before taking contributions.
Model improvement. Annotate or edit the relevant section live, explaining the effect of each important change.
Require transfer. Students apply the same criterion to their own work or a fresh example, then you sample the resulting improvement.
example: A teacher projects an anonymised paragraph that has a strong claim but a weak explanation. Pupils inspect the criterion, then watch a live edit and explain why it improves the link. Everyone makes an equivalent improvement in their own response. The projected work creates shared learning rather than a public judgement of its author.

title: Clear instructions and front-loading: specify participation before the task

links.label: Barton — Front-load the means of participation

intro: Use front-loading when students begin responding or moving before they have heard the participation instructions. Say how to respond before giving the content that will capture attention.
tips: Put participation first. “On your board, silently…” comes before the question, not after an answer has been called out.
Keep the instructions numbered. Students can retrieve the first action and the checking point more easily than a long paragraph of directions.
Use an Instruction Sandwich. State the instruction, check that students heard it, then restate the concise version before release where useful.
Display complex directions afterwards. A stable reminder can support action without competing with the original spoken message.
Use a clear release cue. “When I say go” separates listening from movement and prevents the first instruction being lost.
script: “In silence, write one answer on your board and keep it hidden. What are the two response rules? Now the question: which source is more reliable?”
do: Specify where, how and when students respond.
Check listening before students act.
avoid: Asking the question and adding instructions afterwards.
Repeating every direction automatically without finding out what was missed.
steps: Plan the action. Define the response location, participation mode, stopping point and what students should do if finished or stuck.
Secure attention. Use the shared signal and wait until students can access the instruction.
Front-load participation. State how students will respond before presenting the interesting question, object or task.
Check receipt. Ask a student to state the first action or a key restriction, clarifying briefly where needed.
Release clearly. Use the agreed cue, display any useful reminder and observe the first actions before moving into individual support.
example: Before displaying a diagnostic question, the teacher states that pupils will choose silently on boards and keep answers hidden. A listening check retrieves those rules. The question is then shown and the class commits privately. The interesting content has not arrived before the participation instructions, reducing unwanted calling out and contaminated responses.

title: Habits of attention: teaching purposeful listening routines
intro: Use habits of attention to teach where students should direct attention during explanation, modelling and discussion. Each habit needs a learning purpose and a recognisable cue.
tips: Explain the purpose. A listening or viewing action is useful because it supports access to the idea, not because it looks compliant.
Name the relevant focus. Attention may belong on the model, speaker, diagram or text at different moments.
Practise the transition. Students need to switch attention fluently between writing, talk and shared explanation.
Check the message. Recall or application tells you more than posture, silence or nodding.
Avoid a rigid posture test. Use accessible ways of attending and do not treat direct eye contact as the only valid evidence.
script: “For this demonstration, put your pen down and attend to the diagram. Afterwards I will ask you to explain what changed between the two stages.”
do: Teach the action and its purpose.
Make the change of attentional focus explicit.
avoid: Enforcing a posture checklist for its own sake.
Expecting attentional routines to compensate for unclear explanation.
steps: Explain the learning purpose. Connect the habit to hearing a step, following a model, respecting a speaker or reducing distraction—not obedience for its own sake.
Select the highest-value behaviour. Teach only what matters in the current phase, such as tracking a model during explanation or orienting to a peer during discussion.
Model and rehearse briefly. Show what the habit looks and sounds like, practise once and return quickly to the learning.
Reinforce with short cues. Prompt early and quietly, narrate success occasionally and avoid turning the routine into constant commentary.
Apply selectively and adapt the form. Turn the habit off when pupils should read or write; make reasonable adjustments while preserving the attentional purpose.
Fade towards independence. Reduce verbal prompts to a gesture or question so pupils increasingly manage their own attention.
example: In Drama, pupils shift from performance rehearsal to watching a demonstration. The teacher specifies the feature to attend to, then asks pupils to recall the key action and apply it in rehearsal. The attention habit supports access to the demonstration; visible posture alone is not treated as evidence that the performance technique was learned.

title: Classroom transitions: moving smoothly between learning activities
intro: Use a taught transition to move students from one activity to the next without losing attention or learning time. Specify how to stop, shift resources and begin the new demand.
tips: Teach the transition as content. Model and rehearse the exact sequence before relying on it.
Prime the stopping point. Warn students what will happen and what their first next action will be.
Reduce simultaneous demands. Equipment movement, instructions and new subject content should not all compete at once.
Diagnose the failure. Students may not know the routine, or may know it but not yet perform it fluently.
Rehearse the troublesome component. A brief practice of resource return or partner rotation can solve more than a general reminder.
script: “In ten seconds, stop the discussion. Keep the chairs where they are, face the board and wait for the next instruction.”
do: Use clear stop and start cues.
Protect the first moments of the new task.
avoid: Assuming the routine is obvious.
Giving new academic instructions while equipment is moving.
steps: Teach it before using it. Name the transition, explain why it matters, model an example and non-example, and rehearse the sequence with feedback.
Precorrect immediately before the moment. Remind pupils what will stop, move, remain in place and begin; keep the cue brief and positive.
Reinforce the exact success. Describe the efficient, calm behaviour worth repeating rather than offering generic praise.
Actively supervise. Stay visible and mobile, scan likely breakdown points and avoid using transition time for administration.
Revisit and reteach. Refresh after holidays, timetable changes, new pupils or early signs of routine drift; distinguish an unlearned skill from inconsistent performance.
example: A Product Design transition moves pupils from drawing to collecting materials. The teacher primes the stop, gives one resource action at a time and rehearses the route beforehand. Students know where to place unfinished work and when to start again. Practical logistics do not compete with the explanation of the next learning task.

title: Precorrections: preventing predictable problems before they start
intro: Use a precorrection when a predictable situation repeatedly produces the same difficulty. Prompt the desired action immediately before that moment, using the pattern you have noticed.
tips: Be specific about the pattern. Identify when, where and what goes wrong so the reminder is targeted.
Name the action you want. “Carry the tray with both hands” gives more useful information than “Don’t mess about.”
Time the cue carefully. A reminder well before the risky moment may no longer be available when needed.
Adjust the setup too. Resource placement or task clarity can remove a recurring obstacle.
Fade the reminder. As the routine becomes fluent, reduce spoken prompts to a gesture or no prompt.
script: “Before the trays move, carry yours with both hands and walk directly to your bench. We practised this route; use it now.”
do: Prompt a taught action just before it is needed.
Reinforce the successful response.
avoid: A threat presented as a reminder.
Repeating a generic warning without identifying a pattern.
steps: Spot the pattern. Identify when, where, with whom and after what trigger the behaviour reliably occurs; act on a pattern, not an isolated bad day.
Name the replacement behaviour. Describe what pupils should do in positive, specific and observable language that is incompatible with the problem behaviour.
Adjust the setup. Change seating, resources, timing, task design or the physical environment so the expected response becomes easier.
Rehearse and prompt at the right time. Ask pupils to recall the routine shortly beforehand, then use a brief word, gesture or visual cue at the point of action.
Reinforce and check. Name successful enactment, monitor whether the pattern changes and reduce the prompt from a sentence to a gesture to nothing as fluency grows.
example: A teacher notices that a familiar equipment transition repeatedly produces crowding. Just before it, the teacher reminds pupils of the taught collection route and adjusts the location of the resources. Successful execution is recognised. As the route becomes fluent, the spoken reminder is shortened and eventually removed.

title: Making participation safe: prepare, rehearse and respond warmly
intro: Use safe participation routines when fear of public error prevents students from contributing. Pair challenge with preparation and respond to uncertainty in predictable, respectful ways.
tips: Prepare before public response. Silent thinking, writing and paired rehearsal give students something to contribute.
Make error responses predictable. Explain how you will prompt, model or return after an uncertain answer.
Preserve challenge. Safety means students can attempt demanding learning without humiliation, rather than avoid participation.
Deal with ridicule promptly. Peer laughter or dismissive comments undermine the willingness to reveal thinking.
Recognise the learning move. Praise useful reasoning, revision or persistence precisely rather than celebrate confidence alone.
script: “Everyone will have time to think and rehearse. I will ask different people to share. If an answer is uncertain, we will work with it and give you another chance.”
do: Pair high expectations with preparation.
Treat errors as useful information.
avoid: Cold calling as a public trap.
Allowing uncertainty to become permanent opting out.
steps: Build structural foundations. Establish predictable lesson routines, respectful listening agreements and a shared understanding that errors are information for learning.
Prepare before public response. Give thinking time, jotting, a model, guided practice or paired rehearsal so every pupil has something meaningful to contribute.
Make participation predictable. Front-load how pupils will respond, use warm cold call and structure the size or sequence of the public contribution.
Respond supportively to attempts and errors. Acknowledge the useful starting point, clarify the task or thinking and invite refinement without judging the pupil’s ability.
Maintain challenge and accountability. Use prompts, second chances and gradual release to enable success; do not protect pupils by excluding them from the central thinking.
example: A teacher prepares pupils with a written first thought and partner rehearsal before public questioning. When an answer is uncertain, a predictable prompt and later return provide another chance. Peer ridicule is addressed immediately. Students continue to face demanding questions, with a classroom routine that makes revealing uncertainty safer.

title: Everyone–Together–Anyone: planning participation for the whole class
intro: Use Everyone–Together–Anyone to plan how all students think, rehearse and remain accountable. Choose a participation sequence that serves the learning rather than rely on confident volunteers.
tips: Begin with Everyone. An independent thought, jot or board response prevents the first speaker supplying everyone’s answer.
Make Together purposeful. Partner talk should compare, explain or refine the thinking generated first.
Use Anyone for accountability. Select a prepared student to share and involve listeners in evaluating the response.
Choose the sequence for the task. Brief recall may use a different combination from extended reasoning; the framework is not a compulsory three-stage script.
Inspect thinking as well as activity. Busy talk or moving pens can still hide copied or shallow responses.
script: “Everyone write a first explanation. Together, compare the evidence with your partner. Anyone may then be asked to explain which idea you kept and why.”
do: Plan the cognitive action for every pupil.
Keep participation and diagnosis distinct.
avoid: Volunteer-only questioning.
Treating visible participation as proof of understanding.
steps: Everyone thinks. Begin with silent solo thinking or Everybody Writes when the question requires an original response.
Together rehearses. Give partners a precise prompt, a short time limit and a listening expectation.
Anyone shares. Cold call individuals to report their own answer, their partner’s reasoning or a refined joint response.
Everyone remains accountable. Invite pupils to compare, restate, improve or show a final independent response.
example: A lesson first asks every pupil to write a proposed explanation. Partner talk then compares the evidence, and selected pupils share their reasoning. The teacher follows with an individual check where diagnosis matters. The participation sequence involves everyone without confusing a successful discussion with proof of each pupil’s independent understanding.

title: Second Chance / No Opt Out: returning after ‘I don’t know’
intro: Use Second Chance when a student’s first response is “I don’t know” or incomplete. Provide a route to a successful contribution and return to the student.
tips: Signal the return. The student should know they will have another chance and what to listen for.
Give a meaningful listening task. Ask them to select, paraphrase or develop a useful answer rather than repeat sounds mechanically.
Provide help when knowledge is missing. A prompt or model may be necessary before a successful response is possible.
Keep the tone warm. The purpose is continued participation and learning, not exposing hesitation.
Ask for application where appropriate. A further related question can distinguish hearing another answer from understanding the idea.
script: “I will ask two more people, then return to you. Listen for which explanation uses the key term accurately. You will tell us which one you chose and why.”
do: Return after preparation or support.
Require an attainable, meaningful contribution.
avoid: Moving on and never returning.
Repeatedly demanding an answer without giving access to it.
steps: Set the expectation in advance. Explain that an uncertain pupil will receive more thinking time and be asked again after hearing one or two responses.
Pause and reframe. Acknowledge the hesitation without blame, state that you will return and give a precise listening task.
Invite useful peer responses. Ask one or two pupils for clear answers or reasoning that the original pupil can evaluate—not a long parade of guesses.
Return and require retrieval. Ask the original pupil to paraphrase, select the strongest response, explain why or add an idea of their own.
Reinforce persistence and improve. Acknowledge that the pupil stayed with the thinking, then give a task-focused prompt that increases precision next time.
example: A pupil cannot initially explain the selected method. The teacher asks the pupil to listen to two alternatives, then returns for a choice and reason. A further related example follows where useful. The return keeps the pupil engaged in thinking while support makes the expected contribution attainable.

title: Oracy for learning: teaching speaking and listening explicitly
intro: Use oracy routines to teach speaking and listening as skills that support disciplinary thinking. Clarify whether students are exploring an idea or presenting a developed explanation.
tips: Teach the language. Sentence stems and key vocabulary can help students articulate a complex relationship without supplying the content.
Make listening active. Partners can restate, build, question or challenge using evidence.
Distinguish exploratory from presentational talk. Tentative ideas and a polished explanation have different purposes.
Rehearse a specific talk move. Practise giving evidence or disagreeing respectfully before expecting an extended discussion.
Follow with writing where useful. A short revised explanation can consolidate what the talk clarified.
script: “This is exploratory talk. Offer an idea, ask a question and revise your explanation if the evidence changes your view. Afterwards, write the conclusion you can justify.”
do: Teach both speaking and listening explicitly.
Connect talk to the subject learning.
avoid: Assuming fluent speakers already reason well.
Unstructured conversation without a cognitive purpose.
steps: Build stable routines. Use predictable partners and explicit listening norms so transitions are quick and expectations are equitable.
Protect thinking before talking. Give pupils silent time to retrieve, annotate, select evidence or draft a first sentence.
Structure the cognitive question. Specify what pupils must explain, compare, justify or improve—not merely that they should discuss.
Provide the language or stimulus. Use a concrete example, text, image, sentence stem or target vocabulary when it helps pupils express the same ambitious idea.
Create listening accountability. Ask partners to restate, challenge or build, then cold call pupils to share their own or their partner’s thinking.
example: In Social Sciences, pupils use exploratory talk to test an explanation, ask for evidence and revise a tentative claim. A later presentational response requires a coherent conclusion using disciplinary vocabulary. The teacher models the listening and questioning moves, so talk quality is taught rather than assumed from the presence of discussion.

title: Everybody Writes / Silent Solo: thinking in writing before discussion
intro: Use Everybody Writes or Silent Solo when students need to form their own response before discussion. Writing gives quieter students a prepared idea and makes initial thinking visible.
tips: Keep the first write bounded. A claim, two reasons or a first decision is often enough to prepare discussion.
Protect silence. The purpose is individual generation before a partner’s response influences the starting idea.
Choose a prompt worth writing. A trivial question may not need this preparation; reasoning benefits more.
Use the writing afterwards. Ask students to compare, refine or explain their first response rather than abandon it.
Build read–write–discuss–revise. The final revision captures what the discussion added and makes changed thinking visible.
script: “Write your own claim and one piece of evidence before speaking. Compare with your partner, then revise the explanation in a different colour and explain the change.”
do: Require everyone to commit an initial idea.
Connect writing to later talk and revision.
avoid: Allowing partner discussion during the individual stage.
Asking for writing that never informs the next task.
steps: Set the cognitive prompt. Choose a question requiring a claim, explanation, comparison or decision that students have the knowledge to attempt.
Specify the product. State how much to write and the important feature, so preparation does not become an unbounded essay.
Protect independent time. Students write silently without seeing another response or a model answer.
Use the written thinking. Compare in pairs, sample responses or project a useful contrast while keeping listeners accountable.
Revise deliberately. Students improve their own response and identify the reason for a change, preserving the learning gained from discussion.
example: Before debating a historical claim, every pupil writes a position and supporting evidence. Partners compare the reasoning, then pupils revise their own statement and explain the change. The written first attempt protects independent thought; the final revision captures what the discussion added instead of leaving the learning inside an unrecorded conversation.

title: Explaining with precision: plan, sequence and rehearse the explanation
intro: Use precise explanation when the content is correct but the message is too long, unclear or difficult to follow. Plan what to say, what to show and what to leave out.
tips: Rehearse the difficult sentence. A brief rehearsal often exposes vague terms, unnecessary detours and an overloaded sequence.
Funnel attention. Align your words, pointing and visual display so students know which feature matters now.
Use consistent terminology. Switching casually between labels can create extra interpretation work for novices.
Capture the key idea. A stable sentence, diagram or checklist supports early practice after the spoken explanation ends.
Check receipt and application separately. A listening check and a fresh example answer different questions about the explanation.
script: “This arrow shows the transfer, not the store. Watch the arrow while I explain the movement. Now tell me what the arrow represents before we consider a new example.”
do: Plan a concise sequence and useful representation.
Pause between coherent chunks.
avoid: Adding interesting detail that distracts from the main idea.
Reading dense slide text aloud while students try to read it.
steps: Define the core idea. Write the smallest accurate explanation that makes the intended relationship clear.
Sequence the components. Introduce necessary terms and prerequisites before adding the dependent idea; use a concrete example.
Align the representation. Plan the diagram, worked step or demonstration and where students should look at each moment.
Deliver and pause. Use concise language, check listening and allow reading or processing before introducing another component.
Capture and rehearse. Leave a useful summary, guide a related attempt and repair the precise point the responses reveal.
example: A Science teacher rehearses a concise explanation of a particle relationship, chooses a simple diagram and plans two pauses. Students first retrieve a key statement, then apply it in a new situation. A common error leads to a focused contrast. The explanation remains precise rather than expanding into several distracting related topics.

title: Cognitive simplicity: designing slides and resources that support attention
intro: Use cognitive simplicity when slides or resources compete with the explanation. Reduce unnecessary searching, reading and distraction so students can attend to the content that matters.
tips: Remove decorative competition. An irrelevant picture or animated effect can attract attention away from the learning feature.
Place related information together. Keep a label beside its diagram feature and a condition close to the step it affects.
Reveal deliberately. A completed diagram or crowded page may demand more processing than the current explanation requires.
Stop talking over new reading. Give students time to inspect substantial unfamiliar text before explaining it.
Preserve useful reference material. Simplicity does not mean removing the model or vocabulary students need to practise successfully.
script: “Read these two sentences silently first. I will then explain the distinction. Watch the highlighted phrase as we connect it to the diagram.”
do: Use layout and sequence to direct attention.
Keep text and visuals purposeful.
avoid: Decorative images, clutter and redundant text.
Removing essential information merely to make a slide look sparse.
steps: Identify the essential information. Decide what students need to see, hear or read at the current point.
Remove competing material. Delete decorative elements, irrelevant detail and duplicated language that adds no explanatory value.
Reduce searching. Group related content, label clearly and keep the important feature easy to locate.
Sequence the reveal. Introduce information in coherent chunks and separate reading, listening and copying when they would compete.
Test the resource. Check readability from the back of the room and whether students can locate the reference needed during practice.
example: A teacher removes an unrelated image, moves labels beside the diagram and reveals one part at a time. Students read a short definition in silence before the teacher explains its connection to the visual. The revised resource reduces competing demands while retaining the reference information pupils need during practice.

title: Live drawing: building a representation step by step
intro: Use live drawing to build a representation in the same sequence as the explanation. Clarity and purpose matter more than artistic polish.
tips: Start with the meaning. Decide which relationship the diagram will explain before deciding how attractive it should look.
Rehearse the strokes. Plan the order so the emerging drawing supports the spoken sequence.
Label gradually. Keep words close to the relevant part and pause while students read them.
Use pointing and tracing. Show how an arrow, boundary or connection represents the concept.
Ask students to recreate meaning. They can complete a missing part or explain a relationship rather than merely copy the finished picture.
script: “I will add one arrow at a time. Explain what this connection represents before I draw the next one. Then complete the missing part on your own diagram.”
do: Build the diagram in coherent stages.
Rehearse the relationship it represents.
avoid: Complex artwork that hides the concept.
Drawing every label before students know what to attend to.
steps: Connect and display. Start with a blank surface, confirm visibility and link the representation to relevant prior knowledge.
Draw and label gradually. Narrate the concept as each element appears; keep the visual simple and essential.
Pause and read. Stop speaking while students read labels or annotations so verbal and visual information do not compete.
Explain and point. Trace arrows, point to the current feature and check understanding before adding more.
Recreate and rehearse. Students copy, label, predict or explain the representation so the task is active rather than observational.
example: In Geography, a teacher draws a simple process diagram in the order events occur, adding arrows and labels gradually. Pupils explain each connection before completing a missing stage independently. The drawing makes the causal sequence visible; students are not judged on reproducing an artistic copy of the finished diagram.

title: Storytelling and analogies: making an explanation coherent and memorable
intro: Use a story or analogy when it clarifies a sequence, relationship or abstract idea. Keep the narrative tied to the disciplinary meaning students must learn.
tips: Keep cause and consequence visible. A story should help explain why an event or change occurs, not merely entertain.
Map the analogy explicitly. State what each part represents in the target idea.
Name the limits. Tell students where the familiar comparison stops being accurate.
Remove unnecessary detail. Interesting characters or episodes can become the remembered feature instead of the concept.
Return to subject language. Students need to explain the idea without relying on the story alone.
script: “Think of this as a pressure cooker building tension. In the text, what represents the pressure? Where does the analogy help, and where does it stop being accurate?”
do: Choose a narrative that carries the intended explanation.
Connect it back to precise vocabulary.
avoid: A memorable story with an unclear learning point.
Treating an analogy as literally identical to the concept.
steps: Identify the relationship. Decide what the story or comparison will make easier to understand.
Select a familiar structure. Use a short sequence or analogy students can follow without extensive new background.
Explain the mapping. Link the important narrative features to the subject concept and show the cause or relationship.
State the boundary. Identify a way the analogy differs from the target idea before that difference becomes a misconception.
Translate back. Ask students to explain the concept in disciplinary terms and apply it to an example outside the original story.
example: An English teacher uses a short analogy to explain mounting tension in a text. Each part of the comparison is mapped to evidence, and a limitation is named. Pupils then explain the tension using subject vocabulary and quotations. The analogy helps access the idea without becoming a substitute for precise textual analysis.

title: Micro-decisions: notice, interpret and respond in the moment
intro: Use micro-decisions to make teaching responsive while the lesson is unfolding. Notice a useful signal, interpret its likely cause and choose a proportionate next action.
tips: Know what you are looking for. A planned misconception or key decision makes observation more useful than a general scan for engagement.
Probe before changing course. A correct answer may need reasoning; a wrong answer may be a slip rather than a shared misconception.
Find the missing thinking. Ask whose response is absent before judging the whole class from the visible few.
Make the smallest effective change. A cue, shorter step or clearer representation may be sufficient without restarting the lesson.
Check whether it landed. The next response should test the issue that prompted the adjustment.
script: “I can see correct answers, but the explanations use different rules. I will ask for the reasoning before deciding whether we are ready to continue.”
do: Link the action to an observed pattern.
Recheck the affected learning.
avoid: Changing course because of one unrepresentative response.
Persisting with the plan despite a clear common gap.
steps: Notice. Attend to responses, work, hesitation, explanation quality and participation. Deliberately look for pupils whose thinking is not yet visible.
Interpret. Decide whether the evidence shows a task problem, a process gap, insecure prior knowledge, a misconception or a self-regulation barrier.
Respond. Probe, continue, slow down, re-model, reteach, change the participation structure, alter support or increase challenge according to the diagnosis.
Check. Sample understanding again. A micro-decision is incomplete until there is evidence that the action closed the intended gap.
example: A correct board response is accompanied by an incorrect explanation. The teacher probes the decision, notices the same pattern elsewhere and models the crucial distinction. A fresh check tests whether the reasoning changed. The small instructional adjustment follows evidence rather than the planned pace or the reassuring appearance of correct answers.

title: High success rates: deciding when students are ready for independence

links.label: DistillED — Obtain a High Success Rate

intro: Use success-rate evidence to judge whether practice is productive and students are ready for greater independence. Interpret accuracy alongside reasoning, task demand and the distribution of errors.
tips: Treat percentages as signals. Around 80% can be a useful practical reference in some tasks, not a universal rule or guarantee of readiness.
Inspect what the errors concern. A small minority missing a crucial prerequisite still needs follow-up.
Distinguish accuracy from copying. Success with an identical example or visible answer can exaggerate competence.
Increase challenge when secure. Fade support, change a condition or require explanation instead of assigning more of the same.
Return to the learning. Initial success is a starting point for fluency and later retrieval, not proof of permanent mastery.
script: “The answers are mostly accurate. Before you work independently, explain the first decision on a new example. I will check the remaining gaps while you practise.”
do: Use accuracy, reasoning and task structure together.
Adjust support before repeated failure.
avoid: Mechanical release at a fixed percentage.
Making every practice task trivial to achieve high scores.
steps: Sequence for early success. Teach one manageable component at a time and anticipate misconceptions before complexity is added.
Model and guide. Make an accurate first example visible, then co-construct and rehearse several short examples with high participation.
Check accuracy and reasoning. Use all-pupil responses, short quizzes or sampled work to estimate the class success rate and the pattern of errors.

Adjust support or challenge. Below the productive range, re-model, shrink the step or restore a scaffold. When accuracy is consistently above about 90%, fade support or add depth, variation or transfer.
Reinforce and revisit. Use immediate correction, later retrieval and spaced practice so accurate responses become fluent and durable.
example: Most guided answers are correct, but several students have copied a visible method without explaining the first decision. The teacher uses a distinct example and collects reasoning before release. Secure pupils receive a useful variation while the remaining group gets targeted guidance. Readiness is judged from the demand and pattern, not the percentage alone.

title: Atomisation: breaking learning into prerequisite and new knowledge
intro: Use atomisation in lesson preparation to identify the small pieces of knowledge and action a successful performance requires. Separate existing prerequisites from genuinely new learning.
tips: Start with a real task. A representative example exposes the decisions students actually need to make.
Ask what each step depends on. Reading a symbol, selecting a rule and completing an operation may require different knowledge.
Check prerequisites separately. A complex final question can hide which small component is missing.
Avoid endless fragmentation. Keep the overall concept visible and recombine the pieces after rehearsal.
Use the analysis to plan teaching. Atomisation is useful when it changes the explanation, check or practice sequence.
script: “To calculate this mass, students must interpret the formula, find the amount, use the relationship and manage units. Which are prerequisites, and which are new today?”
do: Identify prerequisite and new components explicitly.
Plan a direct check for the likely bottleneck.
avoid: Reducing the task to disconnected facts.
Assuming a difficult final answer reveals which component failed.
steps: Choose the endpoint. Write a representative question, performance or response that embodies the intended learning.
Unpack the actions. Work through it and list the knowledge, interpretations and decisions required at each point.
Separate old and new. Mark components that students should already know and those the lesson must explicitly teach.
Plan the prerequisite checks. Use short direct prompts, repair insecure foundations and recheck before introducing dependent content.
Build the episode. Sequence the new components, a concise model, guided rehearsal and recombination into an independent whole-task attempt.
example: Preparing a gas-volume calculation, the teacher separates interpreting the question, converting units, recalling the relationship and using the amount correctly. A short check reveals that unit conversion is insecure. That prerequisite is repaired before the new application is modelled. Atomisation changes the teaching route rather than merely producing a longer planning list.

title: Walking-talking mocks: attempt, diagnose, model and re-check
intro: Use an active walking-talking mock to combine expert modelling with student attempts and diagnosis. Give explanation time where the responses show it is needed.
tips: Attempt before the model. Students need a chance to make decisions before seeing the teacher’s solution.
Commit confidence before feedback. A score alongside the answer helps identify confidently held errors for later review.
Scan in zones. Where several staff are present, assign areas so every response can be seen.
Use equivalent follow-ups. A shadow question can check the repaired idea without students simply copying the original.
Make the revision usable. Review Cards give students a question they can test themselves on later.
script: “Try this question first and rate your confidence. Show the first line of working. We will model the part causing difficulty, then everyone will attempt a related question.”
do: Use responses to decide explanation time.
Include a recheck and later retrieval.
avoid: Teacher talk through the whole paper before pupils attempt it.
Giving every question identical treatment regardless of need.
steps: Attempt and commit. Work through one question at a time; students write an answer and confidence rating before any model is shown.
Gather evidence. Use boards for a final answer, first decision or line of working; allocate staff scanning zones where necessary.
Model responsively. Confirm secure work briefly or explain the specific difficulty, making expert decisions visible.
Recheck and stretch. Use a fresh equivalent question after teaching, then a What If variation where the underlying idea is secure.
Create Review Cards. Begin with high-confidence errors, record the mistake and corrected example, and schedule later self-quizzing.
example: During mock review, pupils attempt a question and rate confidence before staff scan boards in zones. A common first-step error receives a short model and a fresh shadow question. Secure answers receive a purposeful What If variation. Pupils then build Review Cards from selected errors instead of leaving only with an annotated paper.

title: Review Cards: turning errors into future retrieval

links.label: Barton — Walking-Talking Mock Exams: Review Cards

intro: Use Review Cards to turn corrected errors into a personal retrieval resource. Separate the question from the solution so students can attempt it again without seeing the answer.
tips: Begin with a high-confidence error. It identifies an important mismatch between certainty and correctness.
Annotate for the future self. Include why the decisive step works and what caused the original mistake.
Add a help reference. Link to an appropriate worked example, revision resource or practice location.
Quiz before turning over. Looking at the solution first turns the card into rereading.
Return errors sooner. A simple deck routine can revisit incorrect cards before secure ones without needing a complex system.
script: “Put the question on the front. On the back, record the topic, your mistake, a corrected worked example and the note that would help you avoid it next time.”
do: Keep the question and solution on opposite sides.
Revisit the cards through independent attempts.
avoid: A card containing only a final answer.
Making cards that students never use for retrieval.
steps: Select the error. Choose a consequential gap from a quiz, assessment or mock, prioritising a confidently held mistake where useful.
Write the front. Copy a complete question or prompt that can be answered independently.
Build the back. Record the topic, original mistake, corrected method and annotations that explain the crucial decision.
Add support. Include a specific reference for help or further practice, checking that the solution is accurate.
Use the deck. Attempt the front before checking the back; revisit incorrect cards sooner and return to secure cards after a longer interval.
example: A pupil turns a confidently incorrect quiz item into a card. The front contains the question; the back explains the mistake, corrected method and where to find more practice. Later, the pupil attempts the front before turning it over. An incorrect attempt returns sooner in the deck rather than disappearing after the original correction.

title: ‘What if?’ questions: vary a condition to deepen understanding
intro: Use What If questions to deepen a secure example by changing one condition. Students should adapt the reasoning they have established rather than begin an unrelated problem.
tips: Change as little as necessary. A small consequential alteration makes the relationship easier to inspect.
Ask for a prediction first. Students can state what they expect to change and what will remain true.
Use Tick Trick thoughtfully. Compare working with the model to identify the decisions or criteria that earn credit.
Reset when needed. A clean, distinct example tests whether students can start the method independently.
Extend after security. A demanding variation is more useful when the basic method is sufficiently understood.
script: “What if this value doubles? Before calculating again, explain which part of your working changes and which part stays the same.”
do: Preserve the underlying concept.
Ask for the reason the answer changes.
avoid: Changing several unfamiliar demands simultaneously.
Using extension while the original decision remains insecure.
steps: Establish a secure example. Check the class can complete and explain the basic method or idea.
Inspect the structure. Identify the steps or criteria that matter, using the model where useful.
Alter one condition. Change a value, representation, requirement or constraint that makes students adapt their reasoning.
Predict and test. Ask everyone to explain the expected effect before checking a calculation or completing the altered task.
